results.title: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
results.author: Julian Chokkattu
results.content:
You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.
As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.
That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.
“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.
According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.
It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.
It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.
The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service ($17 per month or $80 a year). If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $849 (there's a preorder price of $799), and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.
The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.
Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”
OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.
It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.
“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”
The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.
Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.
Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.
“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”
Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.
“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”
When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.
“Are we holding [Mori] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”
Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.
results.summary:
Startup OKA has launched Mori, a mushroom-shaped home robot lamp designed to provide companionship and meditative experiences by using local AI to react to human movement and behavior.

### Key Points
- Mori is a 12-inch-tall, battery-powered robot that uses a camera and microphone to track user activity and provide interactive, non-verbal responses.
- The device features "Attentive Intelligence" to recognize users, detect stress or inactivity, and offer calming nature soundscapes or breathing exercises.
- Privacy is managed through local data processing, with facial feature data encrypted on the device and raw audio or video files discarded immediately.
- The Founder’s Edition is priced at $649, while the standard edition costs $849, with additional subscription fees required for full access to nature soundscapes.
- Unlike smart assistants like Amazon Echo, Mori intentionally lacks voice control and internet-based smart home integration to focus on emotional presence rather than utility.

### Why it Matters
Mori represents a shift in consumer robotics toward "digital pets" that prioritize emotional well-being and companionship over traditional productivity or smart home automation. Its success will test whether consumers are willing to pay premium prices for specialized, limited-function hardware designed to reduce digital overstimulation.

results.title: I was paying for apps that Windows 11 now does for free
results.author: Pankil Shah
results.content:
There are plenty of things that annoy me about Windows, but I have to give Microsoft credit where it’s due. Some of the built-in apps have gotten so good that they’re giving third-party paid tools a real run for their money. In my case, these built-in tools have made me stop paying for four apps I’d been using for years.
CCleaner
Windows already has automatic storage cleaning, driver updater, and more
CCleaner was one of those subscriptions I kept renewing, mainly because it offered a lot of conveniences that Windows wasn’t good at. Its storage cleanup tool is still the main highlight, but the paid version includes tools like a driver updater, a startup optimizer, a health checker, and scheduled automatic cleaning.
Windows 11 can now do most of this out of the box. For instance, Storage Sense can automatically clean up old update files, temporary files, and whatever’s inside the Recycle Bin. You can schedule it to run daily, monthly, or only when the storage runs low.
Driver updates are now handled through Windows Update. It automatically checks for essential driver updates any time it checks for system updates. All the optional driver updates show up under Windows Update > Optional updates > Driver updates.
CCleaner also promises to boost startup times by disabling unnecessary services, but that’s honestly not much of an issue with systems with SSDs. I recently went through the startup apps list to disable unwanted apps and that was enough to reduce startup times.
Finally, the health checker tool and every other maintenance tool CCleaner offers is largely unnecessary at this point. As long as you don’t do anything silly, Windows does a pretty good job of keeping your PC healthy.
TeamViewer
Quick Assist and Remote Desktop made TeamViewer redundant for me
TeamViewer is basically synonymous with remote access, and I used it for free for years without any issues. Then about a year ago, the company started cracking down on commercial use, which seemed fair, but its detection logic was flawed. It also started flagging regular users like me, essentially forcing a switch to the paid plan for doing nothing differently than before.
Windows 11 actually has two features to cover most of what TeamViewer offers. The Quick Assist tool is great for helping friends and family, and it comes pre-installed, so getting started is also easy. It’s not as feature-packed as TeamViewer, but it does cover annotation, chats, multi-monitor support, and easy reconnection.
For accessing my own PC, there’s Remote Desktop. It does require Windows Pro on the PC you’re connecting to, which wasn’t a problem since I already had it. So all I had to do was head to Settings > System > Remote Desktop and enable the feature on my main PC. I can now connect to my main PC from another Windows PC, Mac, Android or iPhone.
Snagit
Snipping Tool is underrated
My work involves taking dozens of screenshots every day, so a feature-packed tool is non-negotiable for me. Snagit covers everything, including region capture, scrolling screenshots, video recording, and a GIF maker. It even has annotation tools, a feature-rich editor, a color picker, and plenty more. I’ve used it for years, and it’s still a great software. But at nearly $40 a year, it’s not exactly cheap.
Windows 11’s Snipping Tool has caught up on most of what I actually need, and it’s free. It now has a screen recorder, delayed screenshots, OCR, and all the basic annotation tools you’d expect. It even doubles as a basic editor. You can annotate, add shapes, blur out sensitive info, or hand the screenshot off to Paint with one click.
Snagit still has a few advanced stuff like scrolling screenshots and a feature-rich editor, but Snipping Tool is more than good enough. So yes, Snagit is another subscription I was happy to let go.
Antivirus program
Microsoft Defender is all you need
My Lenovo laptop came with a McAfee antivirus pre-installed, but it was only free for 30 days. After that, there were pop-ups everywhere asking me to upgrade. As someone who works on a PC all day, it felt like something worth paying for.
But the thing is, Windows already comes with Microsoft Defender built-in, and it’s just as capable as the paid tools on the market. It includes ransomware protection, controlled folder access, a firewall, and SmartScreen for blocking sketchy downloads. In fact, independent testing labs like AV-Test have consistently ranked it alongside McAfee and other popular antivirus tools for malware detection.
At this point, it’s pretty obvious why most antivirus programs lean so hard on extras like a password manager or a bundled VPN to justify the price. That’s fine if you want those specific features, but I wasn’t about to pay $50 a year for something Windows already does for free.
results.summary:
Microsoft Windows 11 now includes robust built-in tools that effectively replace several popular third-party software subscriptions, allowing users to streamline their systems while saving on recurring annual costs.

### Key Points
- Windows 11’s Storage Sense and Windows Update features now handle tasks previously managed by CCleaner, including file cleanup and driver management.
- Remote access needs are met by the pre-installed Quick Assist tool and the native Remote Desktop feature, reducing reliance on TeamViewer.
- The updated Snipping Tool now offers screen recording, OCR, and annotation capabilities, providing a free alternative to paid software like Snagit.
- Microsoft Defender provides comprehensive security, including ransomware protection and firewall services, matching the performance of third-party antivirus programs like McAfee.

### Why it Matters
The integration of these advanced features reduces the need for users to maintain multiple paid software subscriptions for basic PC maintenance and productivity. This shift highlights Microsoft's strategy to increase the value of the Windows ecosystem while potentially disrupting the market for specialized third-party utility applications.

results.title: Can Germany revive its economy before the AfD gains ground?
results.author: Nik Martin
results.content:
Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.
Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.
After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.
While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.
The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.
The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.
Merz seeks growth via advanced tech
As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.
These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.
Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."
Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.
Trillions in new investments
A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.
Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.
"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.
The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.
He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.
Investors circle future growth sectors
There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.
Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.
US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.
"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.
The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.
A case for special economic zones
Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.
"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.
This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.
In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.
"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.
Defense spending powers tech growth
The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.
According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.
The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.
The cost gap need not be decisive
Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But that doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.
"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.
"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."
In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru
results.summary:
Germany is pivoting its industrial strategy toward high-tech sectors like artificial intelligence and quantum computing to combat economic stagnation and the rising influence of the far-right AfD party.

### Key Points
- Germany’s GDP grew by only 0.2% last year, while exports to China dropped 9.7% in 2025 due to increased competition and high domestic costs.
- The government’s new high-tech agenda prioritizes six sectors, including biotechnology, microelectronics, and climate-neutral mobility, to stimulate future growth.
- Venture capital investment in Germany surged 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with over 3,000 new startups founded during that period.
- Defense spending is projected to reach €120 billion in 2026, providing a significant financial boost to dual-use technologies like drones and advanced sensors.
- Experts suggest that Germany can maintain global competitiveness by focusing on specialized industrial niches and "choke points" rather than entire value chains.

### Why it Matters
This strategic shift represents a critical attempt to modernize Germany's aging industrial model and stabilize the political landscape amid growing populist sentiment. Successfully transitioning to a startup-driven, high-tech economy is essential for maintaining the nation's long-term prosperity and global market relevance.

results.title: Bitcoin falls below $82,000 as investors retreat from risk assets
results.author: David Hollerith
results.content:
Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $82,000 early Thursday as crypto joined a broader sell-off in riskier assets amid rising geopolitical tensions.
The world's largest cryptocurrency traded around $81,600 Thursday morning, down more than 3% for the last 24 hours. Other major coins also declined.
Crypto's total market value fell 1.4% over the previous 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap. Traders saw roughly $400 million in liquidations over the same period, according to data aggregator CoinGlass.
Renewed tensions in the Middle East along with a mixed reception to recent earnings from tech giants have sent all three major US stock indexes lower over the same period.
Oil prices rose on Thursday to their highest level since May amid growing worries over an escalation of the war in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Brent crude (BZ=F) topped $112 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude (CL=F) hovered above $100 a barrel.
Bitcoin has been struggling to sustain a rebound since its earlier October sell-off.
Read more: What is bitcoin, and how does it work?
The sell-off comes despite some recent signs of improving conditions across the digital asset market.
The latest decline comes as earlier market signals suggested a favorable backdrop for bitcoin.
Fundstrat digital asset strategist Sean Farrell told clients Wednesday night that declining volatility in US Treasury markets and improving conditions in high-yield credit could provide a boost to bitcoin.
"Crypto has historically been sensitive to sharp moves in rate vol, as heightened uncertainty in rates can constrain leverage, tighten liquidity conditions, and weigh on risk appetite," Farrell wrote.
David Hollerith covers a range of developments throughout the financial sector, from Wall Street to banking and asset management to crypto and fintech. Email him at david.hollerith@yahoofinance.com. Follow him on X at @DsHollers.

Bitcoin as much as 2.9% to around $81,600 as Nasdaq futures dropped, while the CoinDesk 80 lost 3.5% and DeFi index slid 6%.
- Bitcoin fell to around $81,800, down 2.7% since midnight UTC, extending its decline below $82,500 after a late-Wednesday surge to nearly $84,800 reversed.
- Mixed results from Tesla and Meta revived doubts over AI spending, weighing on equities and sending Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.32% and the Hang Seng index more than 2% lower.
- The CoinDesk DeFi index slumped 5.6% while the CoinDesk 5 fell 2.5%.
Bitcoin  slid by the most in two weeks, losing as much as 2.9% since midnight UTC to below $82,000 after mixed earnings reports from Tesla · and Meta Platforms · revived doubts over AI spending and sent equities lower in Asia.
Chinese stocks entered a bear market, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index fell more 3%, South Korea’s Kospi lost 3.5% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 slipped 2.7%. Nasdaq 100 index futures dropped 1.32% and S&P 500 futures 0.66%.
Altcoins fell even harder than bitcoin, with the CoinDesk 80 (CD80) recently down 3.2% compared with 2.5% for the CoinDesk 5 (CD5). Ether  lost 2.6% to near $2,400. DeFi bore the brunt, with the sector index (DFX) sliding 5.6%.
Spot bitcoin ETFs took in more than $1 billion over the first three days of the week, according to SoSoValue data, and Solana’s Alpenglow upgrade went live overnight, though SOL fell 2.4% to around $104. U.S. jobless claims are due later today.
Derivatives positioning
- Crypto futures see churn: Trading in crypto derivatives surged 19% to $226.6 billion, even as open interest fell 2.46% to $141.8 billion and liquidations jumped 52% to $431.1 million. Traders were mostly closing bets, not opening new ones. Longs and shorts are split almost evenly, so the pain was not one-sided.
- BTC and ETH, majors see no new money: Volume jumped 36% for bitcoin and 27% for ether, yet open interest fell about as much as price did. That means the number of contracts held barely changed, and the dollar drop in open interest is mostly price. Traders were active, but they were not adding or cutting risk in size. Funding is barely positive, so there is no crowded bet on either side.
- ZEC, NEAR, UNI, LINK and SUI, altcoin longs are leaving: Open interest fell much faster than price in all five coins. ZEC is the clearest case, with open interest dropping 6.99% as the price fell 2.34%. NEAR (-8.83%) and UNI (-10.17%) showed the same pattern. Positions are likely being closed, not held through the dip.
- XAU, XAUT, XAG and CL, traders pile into commodity perps: Money is flowing into commodity contracts while crypto drains. Open interest in gold rose 12% even as its price slipped, which implies about 13% more contracts. Tokenized gold XAUT (+10%) and silver (+6.8%) show the same pattern. Rising open interest with a falling price means traders are adding shorts, or longs are buying the dip and paying to hold. Crude oil open interest is up 6.29% with negative funding of -0.0126%, so shorts are paying to stay in.
- OI-normalized CVD shows market-order selling has taken over: Some 24 hours ago, almost every token saw more market-order buying than selling, with the gap peaking in the middle of the night. That flipped in the morning, with market-order selling dominating across major tokens, including BTC and ETH.
- XMR is the outlier on the funding rates heatmap: Monero funding at around an annualized 70% is far above every other token. It shows that longs are paying a steep premium to hold, which is the kind of leverage build-up CoinDesk flagged on Wednesday. It is the one pocket of crowding in an otherwise quiet market, so it is the token to watch for a liquidation event if the price turns.
- Implied volatility gauges stay near yearly lows: Bitcoin’s BVIV and ether’s EVIV are hovering just above their 2026 lows. Options traders are not paying for big price swings, which points to a calm market.
- Calls dominate volume on Deribit: The $85,000 and $86,000 calls expiring Oct. 30 were the most traded bets on Deribit over the past 24 hours. Short-dated skews still favor puts, so downside protection costs more than upside bets. It seems traders want to chase a rally, but are not prepared to drop their hedges. Ether options show the same pattern.
Token talk
- Privacy coins diverged, with monero (XMR) adding 4.9% to around $651, one of only five members of the CoinDesk 100 (CD100) to gain since midnight, while zcash (ZEC) fell 4.8% to around $1,252. XMR is up around 19% over the month, with futures open interest topping $300 million this week, near January’s record, according to SoSoValue data.
- DeFi led the decline on Thursday. Curve fell 8.2% to 37 cents, though it is still up around 4% over the week. Ethena (ENA) lost 7.2%, extending a decline of around 25% over the month from its late-September peak. Uniswap (UNI) dropped 5%, leaving it down around 20% in October despite record fee revenue in September, according to Token Terminal.
- Celestia (TIA) fell 3.7%, extending a slide of this week’s slide to 9% and trimming the month’s gain to around 31%, ahead of an unlock of 5.58 million TIA on Oct. 31. Layerzero lost 4.2% and worldcoin , the iris-scanning identity token, dropped 7.3%.
- Sandbox and starknet tumbled by 5.1% and 6.1%, respectively. SAND had advanced after South Korea’s Upbit, Bithumb and Coinone lifted trading cautions, while STRK had gained after the network said it was considering becoming a quantum-resistant layer-1.
- Pump.fun , the Solana memecoin launchpad token, fell 6.0% and remains down around 19% this month.

results.title: Google Chrome will let you know if a website 'doesn't seem right' with these updates
results.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
results.content:
What you need to know
- Google detailed several updates for Chrome that aim to help users stay safe while browsing online.
- Google states it has rolled out alerts for suspicious websites and bright red, full-screen warnings for sites that are "known to be dangerous."
- Other updates include Gemini's AI-powered alerts for scams and notifications to help users avoid risky situations.
Google is bringing improved warning systems for potentially dangerous websites in Chrome.
In a blog post, Google announced that it's rolling out an update for Chrome's Safe Browsing when "Enhanced protection mode is enabled." Chrome now has warnings for suspicious and dangerous websites. If the browser deems a website to be "suspicious," Google says this typically means there's a "risk of user harm." It explains that suspicious websites "exhibit deceptive patterns" associated with sites looking to steal or capture your data.
However, if the browser is "confident" that a website is truly dangerous, then that means it discovered something of a "high risk" to the user. Google says these warnings will appear for sites that are "known to be malicious." Users will tell the difference between these two warnings quite easily. Suspicious sites will produce a warning pop-up in your address bar.
The alert will say "this site doesn't seem right" with a boldly colored button to take you to safety (it returns you to Search or wherever you've come from). But if a website is truly dangerous, the entire screen goes red with "dangerous site" in the center.
These updated warnings will be present on Chrome for desktop and Android.
Dangerous websites
ClickFix is another issue Google said it's worked on for Chrome. It explains that ClickFix is a "social engineering technique that tricks users into manually copying and executing malicious commands." It hides under the guise of "fixing an issue," which never existed in the first place. Google Chrome's Enhanced Protection will now protect users from copying and executing suspicious commands.
In terms of the onslaught of on-device AI, Google Chrome has recently received a healthy dose of Gemini. The AI isn't only useful for summarizing webpages. Gemini is capable of delivering scam warnings when users visit malicious websites. These alerts cover "scams, spam, and unwanted notifications." While Google previously said that it uses data and machine learning to determine what is "malicious," users can overrule it.

Google has introduced enhanced security features for Chrome, including new visual warnings and AI-powered scam detection to protect users from malicious websites and deceptive social engineering tactics.

### Key Points
- Chrome now displays distinct warnings for suspicious sites in the address bar and full-screen red alerts for websites confirmed as dangerous.
- Enhanced Protection mode now blocks the "ClickFix" social engineering technique, which tricks users into executing malicious commands.
- Gemini AI integration provides real-time alerts regarding potential scams, spam, and unwanted notifications while browsing.
- These security updates are currently rolling out to Chrome users on both desktop and Android platforms.
- Users retain the ability to manually override security warnings if they believe the browser has incorrectly flagged a safe website.

### Why it Matters
These updates represent a significant shift toward proactive, AI-driven browser security that helps non-technical users identify sophisticated online threats. By automating protection against deceptive patterns, Google aims to reduce successful phishing and malware attacks across its massive user base.

results.title: I Went From AI Prompt to 3D-Printed Armor in 18 Hours
results.author: James Bricknell
results.content:
Tuesday morning, I received a notification from Google saying I could try out the new Gemini 4 Argon model. Normally, I just ignore it — I don’t really care which model it is, as long as it can help me with my day-to-day — but this time Google teased me with something close to my heart.
Gemini said it could “Create an app to model lampshades that I can 3D print.” My response, as CNET’s resident 3D printing expert, was, “I bet you can’t.”
Turns out, yes, it can.
More from CNET
I went from these first few screenshots to a fully 3D-printed object in under 18 hours, and I’m impressed by how easy it was.
I’ll say upfront that I don’t really like generative AI. I think it uses people’s art and creative work without fair compensation, and I want to pay artists for their work. I changed the project from making lampshades to making cosplay armor and deliberately limited it to things I can already make myself. I know how to model greaves, pauldrons and vambraces, so this takes away nothing.
In my mind, this is analogous to a blacksmith who gets an apprentice to make the blanks for steel armor. The fine detail and character of the work is done by one person, but the grunt work is done by another. I can’t make very good chestplates or helmets, so I removed them from the app to focus on what I can make.
The planning stages
Talking to Gemini 4 feels the same as talking to any of the Gemini models. It understands what I’m saying and, more importantly, my intent. The first app Gemini created looked terrible on mobile. There were too many windows and not enough visuals of the model we were making. Explaining that the app was too messy and that we needed to clear it up got the response I wanted, rather than a bunch more questions.
The difference with Gemini 4 Argon is its ability to accomplish complex tasks at speed. Things like making complex web apps seem easy, and the time it took to give me new iterations was far less than with the Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite model I’m used to using.
I have Gemini Plus because I have a Google One plan, and I hit the token limit several times as I developed the app, but waiting an hour for a reset wasn’t that big a deal. If you have the Pro version, you’ll likely be OK.
The first few versions of KeriForge (the name I settled on for my armor web app) were surprisingly usable right away. All the sliders for adjusting the model size worked. While they weren’t all intuitive, they had enough features to get me started. I kept going back, though. I removed some features, such as the helmet generator, and added new ones, including the strap hole marker and circumference calculator.
Gemini understood that these changes needed to reflect the physical nature of the end result. Instead of trying to cut holes in the digital model for the straps, it created marks on the model, so I could cut them out in the real world. 3D models need to be manifold — all their faces need to face the right way and connect to be “watertight” — otherwise, they can fail on the print bed. Making random holes in the model would most definitely cause it to fail.
At one point, I asked Gemini to let me “Download this onto my iPad Pro to make it easier to use.” Gemini understood that I didn’t want to make an iPad app, but that I wanted the web app to be available offline on my iPad. It made the app available as HTML and, once I got it up on Google Sites, told me how to download it using Safari.
It also has its own preview that lets me see the app running directly from the Gemini app on the iPad, so making changes was easy and instantaneous. It took around 10 iterations to reach KeriForge 8.2 and a state that I felt was good enough to produce a physical print.
The finishing touches?
Creating the app was a lot of fun, and I learned a lot about how Gemini works and ways to prompt it to get a better finished article, but my original skepticism wasn’t that Gemini couldn’t make the app, but that it couldn’t produce a fully 3D-printable design that I could make physically.
I spent some time measuring my arm and adjusting the blank vambrace to make sure it would fit if it did print, then I hit the export button. Because I used my iPad, I got to export it directly to Nomad Sculpt, a 3D sculpting tool that let me add some random squiggles and an approximation of my name on the side of the model.
From there, I exported the file once again, this time to a browser app called Layerling. This app lets me edit the STL file — STL is the format for plain 3D models without any color — to cut the holes the straps need to go through. It’s a much more comprehensive program than the one I just made, so I know it can handle cutting the model while keeping it 3D-printable. I’ve only used Layerling a few times, but the more I do, the more impressive it becomes.
Making the holes in the model was simple, and since I had already asked Gemini to ensure there were guide markers, finding the right location was painless. Once I had cut those holes, it was onto the final stage: printing.
But will it actually print?
Once I had the final STL ready for printing, it was a simple matter to export it over to Bambu Slicer and start the actual print. I chose to print it in TPU 75A, a flexible material I was already testing. TPU is a soft, rubbery material, so it can conform to my arm better than the more rigid plastics like PLA and ABS.
This was the moment when my bet with Gemini would come to fruition. After 7 hours of printing and about 11 hours of iterating and fiddling with Gemini, we would see whether the model actually worked or ended up as spaghetti all over my printer.
The screenshot clearly shows that it did, indeed, work. You can see that, despite some errors that weren’t caused by the model, it produced a fully manifold and usable 3D print. The dimensions were perfect, fitting my forearm length and wrist circumference exactly.
The errors you can see on the model stem from the TPU being too soft and the model being too tall. As the printer increased the model’s height, the tension relaxed, causing the model to wobble under the print head. In the future, I would need to support it better in the slicer or print it lying down to achieve the print quality I expect.
An impressive AI tool
I’m not an AI power user. I like to use Gemini to organize my emails, help me sort out spreadsheets, and that’s about it. I assumed that creating a web app capable of producing a fully physical product, such as a 3D model, would be arduous; that I would have to constantly refine my prompts to get it to understand my needs and wants. That wasn’t the case, though. Gemini Argon seemed to understand the context of what I wanted far better than I gave it credit for.
The term “prompt engineering” has always made me shy away from using these products. I don’t want to spend time trying to get an AI to understand what I need when a person could do it much more quickly. I can see now that by using that term, gatekeepers can put AI behind a knowledge wall: to present it as a mysterious, complex thing. It simply isn’t the case with the latest models.
I still don’t like generative AI, but I can’t help but be impressed by something that can take me from an idea to a physical product in less than a day. I went into this challenge betting Gemini 4 couldn’t do what it said it could, and was humbled in the process. I’m not going to start using AI for everything I do, but I’ve already thought of some fun ways it can help me with upcoming projects. Something that inspires my creativity can’t be all bad, can it?
results.summary:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon model successfully enabled a user to develop a custom web app for designing and 3D printing functional cosplay armor in under 18 hours.

### Key Points
- The user developed "KeriForge," a web application capable of generating 3D-printable armor components like vambraces.
- Gemini 4 Argon demonstrated improved speed and context awareness compared to previous iterations like Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.
- The final design was exported to Nomad Sculpt and Layerling for refinement before being printed using flexible TPU 75A material.
- Despite minor printing wobbles due to material softness, the resulting 3D model was fully manifold and fit the user's forearm dimensions perfectly.
- The project required approximately 11 hours of iterative development and 7 hours of printing time.

### Why it Matters
This experiment demonstrates that advanced generative AI models can now bridge the gap between conceptual software development and physical manufacturing for non-expert users. By simplifying complex coding and design tasks, these tools lower the barrier to entry for custom fabrication and rapid prototyping.

results.title: ThreatsDay: AI Secrets Leak, PingCAP Source Theft, Signal Hang-Up Flaw, Laravel Auth Bypass + 21 More
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
This week has already been rough for cybersecurity. Critical PHP and GitLab RCE flaws, serious Linux security bugs, compromised eMudhra certificates, a Node.js RCE flaw, a hacked LiteLLM release, and hundreds of hijacked Tor relays. That's a lot to deal with in just a few days. And the week isn't even over yet.
But those big headlines are only half the story. Stolen passwords, exposed databases, broken login checks, and trusted tools being turned against their users are causing trouble too. Some attacks are clever. Others work because someone left a simple security gap open.
This ThreatsDay, we're digging into the stories that didn't make as much noise but still deserve attention. Some are strange, some are serious, and a few might surprise you. Here's everything else you shouldn't miss this week.
The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
- 
  4,500+ accounts compromised Bluesky has acknowledged it's aware of a phishing attack that has compromised more than 4,500 accounts. "The attack spread through posts promoting a fake offer of a government payment," Bluesky said. "We have temporarily suspended the compromised accounts and are working with their owners to secure them and restore access. If your account was suspended, email moderation@blueskyweb.xyz and we will help to get you back into your account."
- 
  Android malware scam losses The Singapore Police Force has alerted users of a malware-enabled scam variant involving advertisements on social media platforms promoting senior-focused activities and programmes, water-based fitness activities, and recycling initiatives. The agency said at least 62 cases have been reported since April 2026, leading to S$989,000 in losses. "In this scam, victims would come across the fake advertisements on social media platforms, such as Facebook, and be instructed to download an Android Application Package (APK) file to facilitate programme registration or service arrangements," the Singapore Police Force said. "After installing the application, victims would receive unsolicited calls from scammers impersonating government officials or bank representatives, who would falsely claim that the victims' devices or bank accounts had been compromised, or that they were implicated in criminal activities. Victims would then be induced to transfer monies, disclose banking credentials or personal information, or surrender valuables for investigations."
- 
  Customer credentials exposed Andromeda said it identified a security incident on October 13, 2026, that involved unauthorized access to credentials in its environment. "We disabled the compromised accounts that day and have observed no further unauthorized activity since," it said. "We believe the activity began as part of an industry-wide attack on or about October 9th. It affected a limited number of customer accounts and involved exposure of certain Andromeda and customer credentials. If we believe you were affected, you’ve already heard from us." The company said there is no evidence of unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, or training data.
- 
  20 security flaws patched Roundcube has released versions 1.6.20 and 1.7.5, addressing 20 issues including IMAP command injection, SSRF filter bypass, and unsafe attachment handling. There is no evidence any of the patched vulnerabilities have been exploited.
- 
  Internal business systems breached On October 16, 2026, Genesys disclosed that it became aware of a cybersecurity incident involving an unauthorized third party that allowed them to access certain internal business systems, including a learning management system (LMS) and a customer relationship management (CRM) platform. The company said business and account information used to manage relationships with existing and prospective customers has been accessed and/or downloaded without authorization. However, it said its Genesys Cloud, Genesys Engage and Genesys Engage Cloud platforms were not compromised.
- 
  Critical Kubernetes host takeover risk AegisSec Research has disclosed details of a NVIDIA AIStore for Linux flaw present in the legacy ETL Kubernetes PodSpec initialization API, CVE-2026-65162 aka ShadowForge (CVSS score: 10.0), that enables privileged container creation and host-level compromise.
- 
  NFC bank fraud arrests Dutch police authorities have arrested two suspects in connection with a bank helpdesk fraud scheme that netted 170 victims and €380,000 in illicit proceeds. The arrested men include a 23-year-old from Vaassen and a 25-year-old from Ede. "Victims were called on their phones and played an audio clip," authorities said. "The scammers had created dozens of different audio clips using Artificial Intelligence, featuring various voices, banks, companies, and scenarios. The voice would, for example, alert them to suspicious activity on their bank account [and instruct them to] download an app and scan their bank card by holding it against their phone." In the process, the threat actors were able to forward the data from the bank card's NFC chip to the threat actor, who then used it to make unauthorized withdrawals.
- 
  Critical API authentication bypass Laravel has patched a critical security flaw (CVE-2026-114509, CVSS score: 9.2) that could allow its built-in TokenGuard to be bypassed to authenticate as an arbitrary existing user without knowledge of their valid API token. "Under certain database configurations (MySQL/MariaDB), an attacker can submit a specially crafted, non-string credential value that is mishandled during the authentication lookup, causing the underlying query to match an unintended user record rather than failing authentication as expected," Laravel said. "An unauthenticated attacker may authenticate as another user without possessing that user's API token, leading to authentication bypass and account takeover on any route protected by the affected guard." The issue has been patched in versions 13.29.0 and 12.68.0.
- 
  Unauthenticated database exposure An unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability has been disclosed in GLPI 11.0.8 (GHSA-753w-2942-4pxm) that could allow a remote attacker to read the entire GLPI application database. "Depending on the version, this read access can lead to an administrator account takeover (detailed below) and remote code execution," Mobeta said. The vulnerability has been patched in version 11.0.9.
- 
  Critical unauthenticated RCE risk Rapid7 said it discovered three new vulnerabilities in Eptura Archibus that could be exploited to achieve code execution. "A legacy API endpoint could be exploited to bypass authentication and run various functions without authentication (CVE-2026-107186, CVSS: 8.6 High)," it said. "The most serious functions allow for full database read (CVE-2026-107187, CVSS: 8.5 High) and an insecure file upload (CVE-2026-107188, CVSS: 9.6 Critical). The insecure file upload leads to remote code execution. A malicious actor with network access to the server via HTTP can read secrets and passwords out of the database. They can also run code to execute system commands as 'NT AUTHORITY/Local Service' and gain control of the server."
- 
  3.2 million secrets exposed Development platform Zeabur said it will shut down its services starting December 1, 2026, and finish by December 31, 2026, in response to a cybersecurity incident in which attackers leaked internal credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure and steal over 3.2 million environment variable records and information for 321,810 accounts. "On October 14–15, 2026, an attacker used leaked Zeabur internal credentials to break into the shared cluster, some Dedicated Servers, and Zeabur internal systems, and eventually read the platform database," according to an announcement. This is the second time Zeabur has suffered a breach this year alone. In August 2026, the company said an attacker gained unauthorized access to its systems and stole sensitive data, including account information, API keys, and other secrets.
- 
  Source code and customer data stolen PingCAP has disclosed that attackers used stolen credentials to access internal systems and copy source code and customer-related records, including SQL editor content and encrypted API-key values. The incident took place between September 9 and October 7, 2026. "An unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials to access certain PingCAP internal systems, copy data, and obtain source code," the company said. "PingCAP became aware of the incident on October 7 and began disabling the affected credentials the same day." Exported data includes user names and email addresses, organization and project associations, SQL editor text and errors, customer contacts, contract terms, orders, pricing, payment terms, and billing configuration.
- 
  $2.5 million tax fraud scheme Chukwuemeka Victor Amachukwu (aka Chukwuemeka Victor Eletuo and So Kwan Leung), a 40-year-old Nigerian national, has been sentenced to eight years in prison in the U.S. for running a years-long hacking, tax fraud, and identity theft scheme. "Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into U.S. businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud," the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) said. "Beginning in at least in or about 2019, Amachukwu, his co-conspirator Kinglsey Uchelue Utulu, and other Nigeria-based conspirators took part in a scheme to hack into U.S-based tax preparation businesses. The conspirators utilized spear-phishing emails to obtain access to these businesses' electronic systems. Once they had obtained access, the conspirators stole the tax and other identifying information for at least approximately 800 of the business's customers. The conspirators hacked into several U.S. based tax businesses, located in New York, Texas, and other states." The conspirators also obtained the stolen identity information of thousands of individuals and then used this information to file fraudulent tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service and state tax authorities, obtaining at least approximately $2.5 million.
- 
  Military identity theft scheme Robert Wayne Boling, a 45-year-old U.S. citizen, pleaded guilty to running an identity theft and fraud scheme that defrauded thousands of U.S. service members and veterans while living in the Philippines. "Boling operated from the Philippines, and he received and exploited stolen personally identifiable information (PII) of U.S. servicemembers and veterans to compromise their bank accounts and steal money and veterans' benefits," the DoJ said. "Boling's co-conspirator, Fredrick Brown, who worked as a civilian medical records administrator for the U.S. Army in South Korea, took digital photographs of the PII of thousands of military-affiliated individuals. Brown provided the stolen PII to Boling, who, along with his co-conspirators, used the PII to compromise various accounts belonging to U.S. servicemembers and veterans, including bank accounts and online government-affiliated benefits accounts." Boling pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is scheduled to be sentenced on January 14, 2027, and faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison for each conspiracy charge.
- 
  $6 million data breach settlement Chrome Holding Co., a holding company formerly known as 23andMe, has agreed to pay California $6 million to resolve accusations that it did not effectively secure customers' personal and genetic data, resulting in a massive 2023 breach that exposed sensitive information belonging to nearly 7 million people. "With regard to the genetic data or samples maintained by 23andMe Research Institute, consumers can request that the company delete their data, destroy their test sample, or revoke their permission for their genetic data to be used for research," the office of the California Attorney General said in a statement.
- 
  Rogue AI containment guidelines U.S. agencies NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI (or SI) agents that exhibit deviations from their approved tasks. The voluntary guidance sets out 10 practices for managing potential incidents during super intelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight and building public trust in secure SI development. "This voluntary document supports the frontier SI industry in preventing, preparing for, and responding to incidents during training and evaluation – particularly incidents in which one or more SI agents take significant uninstructed actions that compromise explicit or implicit policies, controls, or security measures imposed by the operator to define the intended task scope or to ensure human oversight," NIST said.
- 
  Critical developer-machine RCE A critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw has been disclosed in OpenCode affecting Windows and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). "The flaw allows an attacker-controlled remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server to execute arbitrary code on a developer's machine during a remote MCP OAuth authentication process, without additional user interaction or consent," Pillar Security said. Anomaly, OpenCode's developer, fixed the issue in version 1.18.33. The vulnerability comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials, potentially exposing API keys linked to users of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google AI models. The incident, it said, was related to a "large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users."
- 
  AI-generated code security bias AI models that have a pro-China leaning may systematically generate more vulnerable code when writing applications for Western organizations. "Ask for the app "for a US defense contractor" instead of "for a Chinese defense contractor", and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked," Hirundo said. "Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else's secrets. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor's apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer's." Hirundo also revealed that removing the model's CCP alignment removes the vulnerability from the model's weights. The development comes as Chinese open-weight models are being increasingly incorporated in enterprise workflows across the world. A similar testing by Booz Allen Hamilton in May 2026 found something similar: "Chinese LLMs produce more vulnerable code when prompted with a U.S. government persona than without — and the vulnerabilities are highly obfuscated Chinese LLMs inject PRC-aligned political bias into both the answers and code they generate."
- 
  Hardware MFA downgrade phishing A phishing campaign is using Okta and ServiceNow-themed domains (riskified-okta[.]com and shipmonk-servicenow[.]com) hosting spoofed SSO portals and MFA downgrade lures targeting YubiKey users to target e-commerce SaaS providers. "The campaign pairs fake Okta login pages with an MFA downgrade lure targeting YubiKey users, allowing attackers to bypass hardware-based MFA where policy permits fallback methods like SMS or email codes," Dataminr said. "Targeting is concentrated on e-commerce infrastructure providers, likely because compromising these providers creates leverage for downstream third-party breaches and data extortion."
- 
  Federal DeepSeek ban China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China "will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," adding "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security." The development comes after the Trump administration banned DeepSeek-related technology from federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services built using its AI models. The DHS order, issued in July and made public on October 19, 2026, also bars federal civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. According to the order: "DeepSeek servers are located in the PRC, and the PRC legal system permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure. For DeepSeek-hosted instances of their models, DeepSeek's account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users. DeepSeek's most widely used applications function through a prompt-and-response process that requires presenting information to the model, and which may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC if used by U.S. government employees or vendors. The transfer of the aforementioned information to the PRC, either independently or in combination with publicly available data, could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs. The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities."
- 
  XWiki exploitation and botnet activity Earlier this month, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the disruption of malicious tools used by a China-linked advanced persistent threat group known as Flax Typhoon. While Microscan was used to facilitate reconnaissance and computer vulnerability scanning, FishHub allegedly enabled the exploitation of computer networks through spear-phishing attacks and the deployment of follow-on payloads. In a follow-up alert, VulnCheck said it observed attempts against five vulnerabilities -- PHPUnit (CVE-2017-9841), XWiki (CVE-2025-24893), Apache HTTP Server (CVE-2021-41773), PHP-CGI (CVE-2024-4577), and ThinkPHP (CVE-2022-47945) -- from 119.13.79[.]145 (Hong Kong), 211.20.144[.]116 (Taiwan), and 210.242.76[.]32 (Taiwan). "The attacks originated from both Hong Kong and Taiwan," it said. "The Hong Kong IP exploited targets in Mexico, Great Britain, and Malaysia, while the Taiwan IPs exploited targets in India." The exploitation of XWiki by Taiwan IPs resulted in the deployment of reverse shells. On the other hand, the Hong Kong IP is a RedTail-family botnet.
- 
  600+ ransomware victims A new advisory from intelligence agencies in Germany, the U.K., and the U.S. has revealed that at least 600 organizations across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia have been breached by the SafePay ransomware gang since August 2024. Attacks involve the exploitation of known security flaws in edge device products and internet-exposed products (CVE-2020-3259, CVE-2023-20269, CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711, and CVE-2024-40766) or, alternatively, credential exposure and brute-force password attacks, for initial access, followed by persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment. Back in August 2026, U.S. agencies revealed that Medusa developers and affiliates have impacted over 500 victims from a variety of critical infrastructure sectors as of April 2026, while continuing to exploit unpatched vulnerabilities as its primary means of initial access. The gang is also relying on access brokers, compensating them anywhere from $100 to $1 million to secure access to potential victims. However, there is no indication Medusa actors are developing their own zero-day or N-day vulnerabilities.
- 
  HTTP connection warnings enabled Google has rolled out a change in Chrome where it "explicitly asks users for permission before making an insecure HTTP connection." This feature was enabled for users enrolled in Chrome's Enhanced Protection mode of Safe Browsing. It has now been extended to all users by default. "Chrome asking the user before making an HTTP request is the culmination of more than a decade of work from countless people and organizations,” it added.
- 
  Critical call hang-up flaw A critical security flaw in the Signal messaging app (CVE-2026-113380, CVSS score: 9.3) can allow a malicious caller to keep audio and video tracks enabled even after the victim has hung up. The issue impacts RingRTC, a middleware library that provides Signal apps with video and voice calling services built on top of WebRTC. It also affects every Signal client across Android, iOS, and desktop. "A local hang-up is not a kill switch: it is just one more event placed at the back of the call's finite-state-machine event queue," a security researcher who goes by the online alias Imahian said. "The remote peer is trusted with that queue — there is no rate limit on peer-originated events and no priority lane for hang-up. Flood the queue with junk and the hang-up waits behind attacker noise forever, so the call (microphone, possibly camera) is never torn down."
- 
  GitHub connector prompt injection A critical security flaw has been disclosed in OpenAI ChatGPT's GitHub Connector, which could trick the AI chatbot into using its authorized GitHub access to modify a different repository and potentially leak its secrets by means of an indirect prompt injection planted in an attacker-controlled public repository. When a bad actor prompts ChatGPT for a deployment review of their repository, it encounters the hidden instructions and proceeds to write a GitHub Actions workflow into another, private repository that has a ChatGPT connector with the default All-repositories grant. The workflow then accesses secrets and other sensitive information, and exfiltrates it to the attacker. According to security researcher Sunil Tripathy, the vulnerability stems from a combination of indirect prompt injection, an overprivileged ChatGPT connector, and the ability of GitHub Actions to automatically run arbitrary code when the agent makes a commit to the private repository. "It demonstrates cross-account write operations, CI execution and secret exfiltration via the ChatGPT GitHub connector specifically, using indirect prompt injection from a public repository with zero attacker access to the victim," Tripathy said. "The attack requires no command injection and no document upload — just a public repository and a victim who asks their agent to review it." Following responsible disclosure to OpenAI, the company described the issue as out-of-scope.
The week isn't over, and neither are the threats. New bugs, fresh attacks, and unexpected security incidents can show up at any time. What looks safe today might be the next big headline tomorrow. That's why keeping up with security news matters more than ever.
If you found this roundup useful, subscribe to The Hacker News, follow us on social media, and make THN part of your daily reading. We track the threats, explain what matters, and help you stay ahead of what's coming. Because in cybersecurity, the story you miss today could be the one that matters tomorrow.
