results.title: LTO roadmap extends to 365 TB per cartridge as tape storage refuses to die
results.author: ashilov@gmail.com (Anton Shilov) , Anton Shilov
results.content:
In a world where SSDs with up to 256TB capacity are about to enter the scene to compete against hard disk drives that store over 40TB, magnetic tape storage may seem archaic. However, the 25-year-old Linear Tape-Open (LTO) format continues to evolve at a rather impressive pace.
The current LTO-10 generation stores up to 40TB of uncompressed data per cartridge, while HPE, IBM, and Quantum — the companies behind the LTO Program — now envision LTO-14 cartridges with up to 365TB of native capacity. But capacity is not the only advantage of LTO. In fact, the consortium has deliberately slowed its capacity roadmap in a bid to prioritize reliability, cost per terabyte, and manageable backup and recovery times over the previous goal of doubling capacity with every generation.
LTO began in 2000 with the LTO-1 format, which stored just 100GB of data natively and transferred it at 20 MB/s. Since then, capacity increased to 200GB with LTO-2, 400GB with LTO-3, 800GB with LTO-4, 1.5TB with LTO-5, 2.5TB with LTO-6, 6TB with LTO-7, 12TB with LTO-8, and 18TB with LTO-9.
The original LTO-10 media introduced in 2025 increased native capacity to 30TB, whereas an extended-length LTO-10 cartridge announced later increased it further to 40TB.
LTO cartridge capacity has increased by a factor of 400 in about 25 years without changing the form-factor itself. For comparison, the capacity of 3.5-inch hard drives increased by roughly 585 times over the same period, from around 75GB in 2000 to as much as 44 TB today, so tape has evolved at a slower pace. However, LTO has evolved without dramatic changes in internal complexity.
Two scaling vectors
The 40TB LTO-10 cartridge is noteworthy because its additional capacity is enabled by higher recording density and literally longer tape. The LTO-10 format uses 15,104 data tracks (enabled by the new barium ferrite recording layer), up 68.5% from 8,960 tracks with LTO-9, and combines them with higher linear density. To make this possible, LTO-10 uses a redesigned high-bandwidth servo system with a low-mass mechanism that enables the head to follow increasingly narrow tracks accurately, including in environments subject to shock and vibration.
Both 30TB and 40TB LTO-10 media use a strontium-doped barium ferrite (BaFe) recording layer, but the 40TB version uses a new Aramid base film that is thinner and smoother and therefore enables manufacturers to put more tape into the same cartridge. According to MagStor, the thinner substrate increases tape length from approximately 1,035 meters with the 30TB cartridge to around 1,335 meters with the 40TB version. Meanwhile, the 40TB cartridge works with the same LTO-10 drives as the existing 30TB media.
Therefore, modern LTO has at least two major scaling vectors: manufacturers can record more bits on a given area of tape, and can put more tape into a cartridge. Meanwhile, with LTO-10, the consortium had to drop backwards compatibility, which we will detail further within this article.
There appears to be plenty of room left on the tape front. Back in 2020, IBM and Fujifilm demonstrated a strontium ferrite tape technology with an areal density of 317 Gb/in², which they said could theoretically enable a cartridge capable of storing 580TB. The prototype used tracks only 56.2nm wide and a 29nm TMR read sensor, which proved that magnetic tape could reach capacities vastly beyond commercially available LTO products.
Capacity is not everything
Ironically, despite considerable technological headroom, the LTO Program has recently made its roadmap considerably less aggressive.
When HPE, IBM, and Quantum extended the roadmap through LTO-14 in 2022, they expected capacity to roughly double every generation. The plan envisioned 72TB for LTO-11, 144TB for LTO-12, 288TB for LTO-13, and a whopping 576TB native — or 1.44PB compressed — for LTO-14. But that changed in November 2025, when the three companies introduced the new roadmap for LTO that significantly slows down capacity scaling. The current roadmap targets 70TB native for LTO-11, 120TB for LTO-12, 210TB for LTO-13, and 365TB for LTO-14.
While the new roadmap is somewhat less impressive, it does not necessarily indicate that tape technology has encountered a physical scaling wall. The developers claim the revised targets are intended to prioritize reliability, affordability, efficiency, and cost per terabyte. The consortium also specifically says that lowering maximum cartridge capacities should help reduce the amount of time required to store and recover data, which is a legitimate argument even though it looks like an attempt to make a 'feature' out of a limitation.
"AI has turned archives into strategic assets," said Stephen Bacon, Vice President, Data Protection Solutions Product Management, HPE. "The new 40 TB LTO-10 cartridge will help enterprise-class organizations — across healthcare, financial services, media, research, manufacturing, the public sector and beyond — consolidate petabytes efficiently, strengthen cyber resiliency with true offline air-gapping, and keep long-term retention affordable and sustainable."
Bandwidth is becoming one of tape's more obvious limitations. LTO-8 offered 360 MB/s of native bandwidth, LTO-9 increased this to 400 MB/s, and LTO-10 remains at 400 MB/s, although hardware compression can boost effective throughput to as much as 1,200 MB/s when data can achieve the assumed 2.5:1 compression ratio.
As a result, while maximum native cartridge capacity increased from 12TB with LTO-8 to 40TB with LTO-10 — a 3.33X increase — native transfer performance improved by only around 11%. At 400 MB/s, writing 40TB sequentially would theoretically take around 28 hours (without the overheads). Future LTO generations will likely increase performance, but the consortium has not yet published transfer rate targets for LTO-11 and its successors.
No backwards compatibility
One thing to note about LTO-10 is that it has broken a long-standing LTO tradition, which is backward compatibility. Up until LTO-7, new drives could generally read cartridges from two generations earlier and write media from one generation earlier. LTO-8 and LTO-9 reduced compatibility to one previous generation. However, because LTO-10 redesigns its head, its backwards compatibility disappears completely: an LTO-10 drive reads and writes only LTO-10 media, although the 30TB and 40TB cartridges are of course interchangeable.
This creates a natural problem for operators that need to maintain archives for decades. Once they adopt LTO-10, they either must migrate all their archives to the new format from LTO-8 or LTO-9 cartridges, or keep the old drives in their fleet, which may be increasingly difficult.
Demand remains strong
Perhaps counterintuitively, the AI boom could strengthen demand for tape. AI infrastructure produces enormous datasets, but not every training dataset, checkpoint, model, log, or generated asset needs to remain indefinitely on expensive SSDs or HDDs.
LTO capacity shipments reached 160.3 exabytes in 2025, down 9% year-over-year. However, shipments in the first quarter of 2026 jumped 57% YoY, according to figures reported by the LTO consortium. The organization attributed the increase to AI-related data growth, traditional archival demand, cyber-resilient backups, continued LTO-9 adoption, and the beginning of the LTO-10 transition.
"We are seeing unprecedented data growth combined with increasing cost, energy, and cyber resilience pressures across the industry," said Hugues Meyrath, CEO, Quantum. "As organizations adapt to this new reality, tape is increasingly viewed as a strategic component of modern data infrastructure, delivering predictable economics and resilient long-term data retention at scale."
Indeed, tape has a number of fundamental advantages that are not going to disappear any time soon. Tape provides vast capacities at a low cost per terabyte, cartridges consume virtually no power while sitting offline, hardware encryption protects data, and physically removing a cartridge from a drive provides a genuine air gap against network-based attacks. LTO also supports the LTFS file system, which maintains indexing information on tape and makes archived files considerably easier to manage.
Meanwhile, tape's disadvantages are equally fundamental and are not going away: tape is sequential and therefore cannot provide anything resembling the random-access performance of HDDs or SSDs. Although nobody expects something similar from it.
LTO isn't going anywhere
25 years after LTO-1 offered 100GB per cartridge, LTO-10 can store as much as 40TB, and the roadmap calls for 365TB with LTO-14 several years down the road. Perhaps more importantly, laboratory demonstrations indicate that magnetic tape itself has considerable scaling potential beyond today's commercial products. Meanwhile, instead of pushing capacity as quickly as technologically possible, the LTO consortium is now deliberately balancing density with reliability, performance, and cost.
For a storage technology which demise has been predicted repeatedly for decades, LTO not only continues to evolve at a predictable pace, but its adoption is growing, while its relevance remains on a high level. Only time will tell whether it remains relevant for another quarter of a century, but its steady progress certainly increases this possibility.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.
results.summary:
The Linear Tape-Open (LTO) consortium is evolving its storage roadmap, prioritizing long-term reliability and cost-efficiency over rapid capacity scaling as it introduces the new 40TB LTO-10 format.

### Key Points
- The LTO-10 generation now offers up to 40TB of native capacity using a thinner Aramid base film and strontium-doped barium ferrite recording layers.
- The LTO consortium has revised its long-term roadmap, targeting 365TB for LTO-14 instead of the previously projected 576TB to improve recovery times and reliability.
- LTO-10 drives have eliminated backward compatibility, requiring organizations to maintain older hardware or migrate existing archives to the new format.
- Despite the rise of high-capacity SSDs and HDDs, LTO shipments grew 57% year-over-year in Q1 2026, driven by AI data growth and the need for cyber-resilient air-gapped backups.
- Tape remains a strategic asset for enterprise data management due to its low cost per terabyte, energy efficiency, and ability to provide secure, offline storage.

### Why it Matters
Tape storage remains a critical component of modern data infrastructure because it provides a cost-effective, energy-efficient, and secure method for managing the massive datasets generated by AI. By prioritizing reliability and manageable recovery times, the LTO consortium ensures that tape remains a viable, long-term solution for enterprise-scale archival needs.

results.title: How the Consulting Class Is Eating the Democratic Party
results.author: Adam Bonica, Jake Grumbach
results.content:
Your phone buzzes with a frantic text message. “DEMOCRACY IS ON THE LINE.” It’s not the first time you’ve gotten a fundraising text like this from the Democratic Party and its candidates. Nor the first time you’ve rolled your eyes. But the ask makes sense. Democracy really is on the line. You have asked yourself what you would have done if you had lived under the authoritarian regimes of the past, and volunteering some time and money seems like the least you could do. You click the ActBlue link and donate $100. The country must be saved, after all.
You, the ordinary American, are expected to step up. But are the party insiders stepping up as well? At the very same moment your $100 clears, the party leadership and strategists are at a donor retreat you were not invited to, walking a few dozen people who write seven-figure checks through the polling and the proprietary model that will set the party’s priorities for the cycle. You have a general sense that this is how the game is played, that winning elections requires money from big and small donors. You’re skeptical of the House and Senate leadership, who are increasingly unpopular with the base. But overall, you see a party apparatus that wants to win and oust the Republican Party from control of government, and you assume both tracks feed that goal.
We’re here to tell you that this view is wrong. The Democratic Party is being devoured by an ecosystem of consultants. Mostly out of view of the party’s voters and activists, political consultants are paid to raise the money, place the ads, and set the strategy. And they’re paid regardless of whether the party wins or loses.
We’ve been studying money in U.S. politics for many years, from uncovering racial inequality in campaign contributions to showing how money in politics helps explain why there are so many lawyers in Congress to studying the feedback loop between wealth inequality, political donations by the ultra-wealthy, and their influence over economic and regulatory policy. More recently, what started as a research project on the exclusion of younger Americans from campaign finance spawned an investigation of what we call “spam PACs” in the Democratic Party fundraising ecosystem. These spam PACs are the groups that raise the bulk of their money by squeezing elderly donors with those high-pressure text messages. What started as a high-volume spam model by a few fundraising organizations in the 2010s has spread to the point that even the Democratic Party’s official campaign committees like the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee are some of the groups that profit most from this strategy. Fundraising spam is destroying trust and enthusiasm for the Democratic Party, driving away young potential donors, and extracting the bulk of funds from a small set of vulnerable senior citizens.
The spam operations are only one half of the problem. The other half is the increasing domination in this realm of an exceedingly small number of very wealthy donors. In the 2024 election cycle, the top 0.01 percent of donors—roughly one in every 10,000 voters—accounted for more than half of all federal campaign contributions. Now billionaires are bankrolling authoritarian consolidation, and the Democratic consultant class has convinced the party that it cannot survive without its own “good billionaires,” as Ken Martin, now the Democratic National Committee chairman, put it while running for that position in early 2025. But this distinction between “good” and “bad” billionaires is probably lost on the 80 percent of Americans who believe big donors have too much influence in politics.
A political party is a vehicle for groups in society—voters, activists, and politicians—to come together to elect representatives who will change the world through public policy and governance. It’s a collective enterprise in which different groups debate and negotiate the direction of the party in primary elections and then come together to take control of government and implement that negotiated agenda. The problem is that the incentives of the Democratic consultant class are not aligned with these goals.
This class—and we use the word “class” intentionally to mean the firms, consultants, and strategists paid millions of dollars by Democratic campaigns to raise money, place ads, and set strategy—is extractive, and this extraction is central to many of the party’s pathologies. Just as a private equity firm buys out a corporation and strips it for parts, the consultant class installs friendly operatives, charges fees, raids the party’s long-term assets, and gives strategic advice that ultimately serves itself over the long-term health of the party.
Our thesis is a simple one: Campaign consultants are businesses that act to maximize profits, and this profit-seeking is often at odds with what’s best to defeat American authoritarianism.
In this piece, we detail how and why the consultant class weakens the Democratic Party. We bring new data analysis showing that there is no meritocracy when it comes to Democratic vendors. They are paid the same whether their candidates overperform or underperform in elections. This same consultant class pushes Democratic campaigns toward short-term money over long-term growth and sells campaign strategies that are lucrative for them but ineffective for the party. In pursuing their financial incentives, the consultant class has reshaped who runs for office, how the party raises and spends money, what it says and claims to stand for, and how it relates to its own supporters. They have made the party older, weaker, less honest, and less capable of fighting the most serious authoritarian threat in American history.
Follow the Money
Let’s begin by following that $100 you donated. We’ve spent the last two years tracing money through Federal Election Commission records, vendor networks, and data on hundreds of millions of transactions. We research money in politics for a living, and we’re used to uncovering troubling realities in the data. But when we traced the Democratic fundraising environment, what we found shocked even us.
If your $100 was in response to a fundraising text or email, the single most expensive way to raise money in American politics, $65 is instantly consumed by the cost of asking you for it. Asking this often, and this aggressively, is expensive. It means paying the data brokers who traffic in your personal information, the digital copywriters who draft the inexplicably bizarre messaging, the email and SMS providers who specialize in slipping past spam filters, the compliance lawyers, and, of course, the fundraising consultants. Another $2 goes to strategic consultants for advice on how to spend what’s left, and $14 to administration, travel, and staff. Of the $19 that finally goes toward advertising for the actual candidate, $6 is skimmed off the top as a placement commission before a single ad airs. In the end, barely $13 of your $100 buys real airtime or digital ads.
Fundraising via text message represents the high end of fundraising costs. Even averaged across all itemized donations, including the wealthy mega-donors writing checks, Democratic campaigns now spend 45 cents of every dollar on fundraising costs, a fourfold increase since 2004. Today’s campaigns like to imagine themselves as efficient machines, remade by big data and microtargeting. In reality, they are less efficient and more extractive than at any point in modern history. Most charity watchdogs will not certify an organization that spends more than 35 percent of its revenue on fundraising. The Democratic Party once cleared that bar, but it no longer does, and for the small-dollar donors it leans on hardest, it isn’t close.
In 2024, Democratic campaigns burned through $2 billion on fundraising operations alone, nearly as much as they spent on advertising. Across both parties, spending on donor contact lists exploded from $20 million in 2004 to $351 million by 2020. Your contact information is a commodity, bought and resold by list brokers who profit not by cultivating you as a reliable member of the party but by churning through you. You are worth more exhausted across 15 campaigns than nurtured by one.
This model selects for vulnerability. A 79-year-old Kansas resident was charged up to 352 times in a single day, and 45,331 times since 2018, for a total of $153,856. A 76-year-old in Connecticut donated 22,335 times for $62,580. There are thousands of cases like these in the FEC records—elderly donors charged dozens or hundreds of times a day by the PACs and candidates spamming them. Federal regulators list “abnormally frequent” transfers by an older customer as a red flag for elder financial exploitation and tell banks to watch for it. In political fundraising, it is now the business model.
The fundraising operations insist they do not target the elderly. But these “whale” donors are what makes fundraising spam viable, and the operators know who they are. And the operation has come at an extraordinary cost. Democrats were positioned for a fundraising advantage that comes along once in several generations. An economic realignment has sent the professional class in metropolitan areas—young lawyers, tech workers, doctors, finance professionals—streaming toward the Democratic Party. Eighty-five percent of millennial and Gen Z donors favored Democrats, a trend that appears durable rather than something they’ll age out of. As this cohort entered its prime earning and donating years, Democrats should have been building the broadest grassroots fundraising base in the history of American politics. Instead, the spam model drove millions of these potential donors away. The party didn’t just fail to capitalize on its generational advantage. It actively destroyed it, trading a rising base that would have funded the party for decades for one that is being exhausted for short-term fees. Private equity firms call this “harvesting.” You stop investing in the business and extract everything you can before the foundation gives way. The consultant class has been harvesting the Democratic Party for over a decade.
Democracy is on the line, the fundraising texts tell us. And the party asks real sacrifices of its own people. Climate activists are told to temper their demands. Trans Americans are told to accept the party distancing itself from their civil rights to chase swing voters. Gaza student protesters are told not to criticize Democrats, even when Democrats fund the policies they’re protesting, and their positions find broad support among Democratic voters. These are painful asks, but they are not out of bounds. Political parties have always had to navigate tensions between their base and the broader electorate. But not everyone is being asked to sacrifice.
The Cure for What Ails You
Whatever survives the fundraising machine enters the second extraction: media consulting. Political media consultants take a placement commission, typically 10 to 15 percent, on every dollar of advertising they place. When accounting for production costs, retainer fees, and other costs, the average percentage going to media consulting firms is actually more like 30 percent.
This media consulting structure comes from a bygone era of commercial advertising. Under the old-school commission model, a company like Coca-Cola hired an ad agency, and the agency would take home a percentage of Coca-Cola’s ad spending as a commission. This created an obvious conflict of interest: The ad agency had an incentive to encourage more ad spending, regardless of its effectiveness. For this reason, commercial advertisers abandoned the commission model decades ago in favor of flat fees and retainers. Where commissions still exist in commercial advertising, they’re tied to the impact of direct ad exposure on “conversions”—but in politics, no one can prove that an ad moved specific votes.
But political campaign ad buys never modernized. Consulting firm income rises with spending, not with success. A consultant who places $20 million in ineffective ads earns twice as much as one who places $10 million in highly effective ads. The incentive is to maximize spending, not win elections.
The first modern campaign consultant in American history was Mark Hanna, who managed William McKinley’s 1896 presidential campaign. Hanna identified the moneyed interests whose fortunes were riding on the ballot and asked for a quarter of a percent of their assets. This raised $3.5 million, nine times what his opponent William Jennings Bryan had raised. Much of this haul was spent printing hundreds of millions of pamphlets, for an electorate of fewer than 20 million people. Hanna’s contemporaries were not impressed. Theodore Roosevelt quipped that Hanna “advertised McKinley as if he were a patent medicine!”
Patent medicines were cure-all tonics of that era, hawked on testimonial and repetition because no clinical evidence of their effectiveness existed. The industry gave rise to the phrase “snake oil,” and the comparison was applied to political consulting from the get-go. In Hanna’s day, the candidate was the patent medicine being peddled to voters. Today, the consulting class has found a better mark. The snake oil is the advertising itself, and they’re selling it to the campaigns. In 1906, Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act, which eventually required medicine to prove efficacy before it could be sold. Political advertising never faced that requirement. It has operated for over a century on the sales pitch of the patent medicine era without ever having to prove it works.
That hasn’t stopped political scientists from studying the effectiveness of campaign ads. Few questions in our academic discipline have been tested as often or as carefully, and the studies have produced one of the most robust sets of findings in the field: Political ads have essentially zero persuasive effect in general elections. The conclusion is among the least controversial statements a political scientist can make, and among the least known outside the profession. A major study conducted 59 randomized experiments on 34,000 voters during the 2016 election cycle, testing 49 real ads from real races. The average effect on vote choice was 0.7 percentage points, and even that was not statistically distinguishable from zero.
The researchers couldn’t rule out that the ads did nothing at all. But the study was designed to test the industry’s fallback claim that ads work under the right conditions. Did it matter if the viewer was a partisan or an independent? If they lived in a battleground state? None of it seemed to matter. Another meta-analysis of 49 field experiments reached the same conclusion that campaign ads and even more personal voter contact had no discernible effect on vote shares. But what about online advertising? A massive 2020 randomized controlled trial involving over 60,000 Facebook and Instagram users found that removing all political ads from users’ feeds had “no measurable impact” on attitudes or voting. If digital ads had meaningful effects, a study this large would have detected them.
The strongest evidence that campaign ads have any effect at all comes from the campaigns’ proprietary data. A team of researchers obtained the complete archive of ad experiments that Democratic campaigns ran through a commercial testing platform in 2018 and 2020, more than 600 real ads tried on half a million people. The ads did move survey responses in the minutes after viewing, by a point or two. But think about how favorable those conditions are. The respondent had just watched the ad with full attention. How many political ads leave an impression that lasts hours, let alone until Election Day?
Even that meager result comes with a troubling caveat for the consulting industry. The researchers then asked the question the consulting fees depend on. Is it possible to predict in advance which ads persuade? They went through all 617 ads and tagged the traits that consultants swear by. Did it make a difference if the ad was negative or positive, angry or hopeful, low or high production values? They checked each trait against the experimental results, 39 comparisons in all. Not one reliably predicted whether an ad moved votes. Traits that seemed to work in one election failed to work in the next one. The industry that bills millions for its expertise does not know a good ad from a bad one. “We find,” these researchers wrote, “that ‘what works’ changes from election to election.” And that only adds to the problem that even “what works” doesn’t work very well.
You may have suspected as much after 2024, when Democrats vastly outraised and outspent Republicans and lost anyway. It’s not that money doesn’t matter at all; it’s influential in primaries, and we are not suggesting that candidates should enter the general with an empty war chest. But the party has to weigh what campaign spending actually buys against what it costs. And the costs are severe. To raise the money, the party resorts to fundraising tactics that enrage and badger many of its own supporters. To court the mega-donors, it softens its positions and shelters insiders from accountability. To spend the money, it funnels billions through a consulting class that takes a cut whether the ads work or not. And in the end, the ads mostly don’t work. The entire apparatus yields a product with little to no measurable effect on general election outcomes.
This raises an obvious question. If money doesn’t win elections, why do candidates debase themselves groveling for five-dollar donations? First, it’s a classic collective action problem: Candidates and leaders want to maximize their own fundraising, even if it harms the party’s long-term goals, because it increases their power within the party apparatus. Second, the consultant class is persuasive. Billions in ad buys justify the aggressive fundraising, the aggressive fundraising fuels the ad buys, and both generate fees. It’s a perfect circle of consultant profit.
The Good, the Bad, and the Generationally Wealthy
These are strong claims, and they’re worth testing against the data. We assembled every contested U.S. House and Senate race from 2012 through 2024, roughly 2,600 Democratic campaigns, along with the vendor payments each one reported to the FEC. That allows two tests. The first asks whether campaigns that spend more on consultants win more. The second asks whether consultants who win more votes get paid more.
The consultant class sells its services on the promise that its expertise helps win elections. Consider the swing districts, where that expertise is supposed to matter most. For each election since 2012, we took the 10 highest-spending Democrats running in House districts where the presidential vote had split nearly evenly. These campaigns spent a median of more than $7 million, most of it on consultants. They did no better than the other Democrats running in the same kinds of districts, who spent less than half as much on consultants. What moved the big spenders’ results was the national waves, not how much they paid to consultants. And among the big spenders, the campaigns that gave consultants the largest share of their budgets won at exactly the same rate as the ones that spent more on staff and other expenses.
The second test turns the question around. Most professional services are hard to grade. Elections are not. Every consultant’s clients win or lose in public, on the same night. If any market could reward good work and punish bad, it is this one. Firms whose clients beat expectations should gain business the next cycle, and firms whose clients collapsed should lose it. We measured each firm’s track record in one election, how far its candidates ran ahead of or behind what their districts would have predicted, and compared it with the firm’s revenue growth in the next. There is no relationship. A firm’s performance in one cycle has no bearing on its billings in the next, and the pattern holds for media firms and fundraising firms alike.
It’s all the more head-spinning to learn how richly this failure pays. When the Democratic National Committee released its autopsy of the 2024 defeat, it omitted a chapter that warned “too many people … have become generationally wealthy off politics and drive too much of the decision-making within the ecosystem,” a system its author called “inflexible and self-enriching.” The FEC records put this in dollar terms. Over the past decade, Democratic candidates and committees have paid more than $5.9 billion for fundraising services, an industry that has more than quadrupled since 2016. The DNC itself spent 17 cents on fundraising for every dollar it raised from individuals in 2006 and is on track to spend over 50 cents this cycle. It raised about as much from individuals in 2022 as in 2010 but spent twice as much to do it. The committee’s well-publicized cash problems this cycle have coincided with massive and growing payments to its fundraising vendors.
Then comes the media consultant’s cut. From 2012 through 2024, Democrats paid media consultants about $5.8 billion, and their cut of 15 to 30 percent comes in between $1 billion to $2 billion, taken for placing ads that move few votes. If you, like many analysts, are concerned about an AI bubble, we’d like to introduce you to the Democratic consulting industry.
The Bad Advice Machine
Campaign managers, strategists, and consultants are rarely, if ever, hired based on their win-loss records. They’re mostly hired for their network. Can they get the DCCC on the phone? Do they have a direct line to super PAC board members? Can they secure list-sharing agreements with ActBlue vendors? Do they have a working relationship with party leadership? Do they get invited on cable news? As our analysis shows, the entire process has little to do with winning or losing elections.
One thing the consultants excel at is making their educated guesswork look like science. For consultants who win big contracts and then lose elections, a scientific-sounding justification for their strategy’s effectiveness is especially crucial. There are a few telltale signs of consultant class pseudoscience: high confidence, no room for uncertainty, and all-too-easy answers to difficult political questions, which usually advise the party establishment and large donors to do what they already wanted to do.
A confluence of trends—including social media, the nationalization of political attention, polling, data journalism, and prediction markets—has made political pseudoscience an easy sell. As a result, we are awash with numbers. Political consultants, pundits, strategists, and party operatives seem increasingly unable to make an argument without them. A campaign should spend more on television because the model predicts a three-point persuasion effect. A candidate should abandon an issue because the cross-tabs show that it performs poorly among independents. A particular message is “validated” because it tested eight points better in a focus group. A candidate is “electable” because a proprietary model gives her a 63 percent probability of winning. A donor should give another $5 million because the data shows that the investment will produce a particular return. A survey experiment that randomly shows different Democratic policy positions on your computer screen is evidence enough that a Democratic candidate can dramatically shift the results of an election if she simply “replac[es] racial preferences in small business loans with preferences for low-income applicants” (this is a real example). Everything has a number, and thus everything sounds scientific.
Political advice used to be openly understood as judgment. Today’s strategist says his consulting firm’s proprietary statistical model shows a 7.4 percentage point advantage of nominating one candidate over another. How he arrived at that number is a mystery to politicians and political scientists alike. But the veneer of precision makes it harder to push back. A candidate can argue with a hunch but not with a model she can’t see inside.
Beyond overclaiming based on flimsy numeric evidence, the other element in justifying all this political snake oil is distress. The consulting class thrives on perpetual crisis. In the world of crisis, Democratic Party politics is not the steady project of organizing and mobilizing Americans into a common project in an uncertain and volatile political environment. Instead, every election requires a massive intervention of new, top-down strategy, which, of course, justifies more consultant contracts.
Consider the “crises” for the Democratic Party in the 2024 election. Gen Z was suddenly “the most conservative generation that we’ve experienced maybe in 50 to 60 years,” according to a prominent Democratic pollster. Other leading strategists proclaimed that increasing voter turnout is now bad for Democrats, a piece of advice so reckless it’s hard to distinguish from sabotage. One New York Times column on how “Democrats Have A ‘Massive Blind Spot When It Comes To Male Issues’” touted the fact that the percentage of men who believe “society has become too soft and feminine” increased from 50 percent in 2016 to 52 percent a decade later, a change within the survey’s margin of error.
These supposed realignments have since dramatically reversed. Gen Z, male, and Latino Americans turned against Trump once they saw Republican economic policy raising the cost of living, mass deportation requiring secret police to abduct noncriminal immigrants and sometimes U.S. citizens from their families, and Republican foreign policy very much not, as JD Vance repeatedly claimed in 2024, put an end to endless war. With Trump underwater with independents by over 50 points in 2026, it would be criminally negligent for Democrats to follow advice to keep voter turnout low. But the overclaims of urgency are the strategist equivalent of the spam fundraising texts: Do what I say, or we perish.
The consultant class’s solution du jour is that Democrats must become more centrist. And fast. To fail to be centrist right now is to cede the republic to corrupt authoritarians. Whether it’s from political consulting firms or pundits, traditional and social media are awash with proclamations that Democrats are too far left, and that moderation is the key to victory. In one example, The New York Times editorial board published a statistical piece that we showed to be based on a statistical illusion.
Academic research on this question tends to find pretty substantial benefits of moderation—but only in the eras before Trump. With Trump dominating politics in an era of populist sentiment, low trust in traditional institutions, new forms of social media, high polarization, and global crises like Covid, academic studies have converged on small or near-zero benefits of moderation. We can’t speak for all academic researchers, but for us, this is a moment to emphasize uncertainty. We’re in a new, volatile era in American politics, and many of the old rules don’t seem to apply. We don’t know exactly what to do, and neither does the consultant class. The difference is, we’re allowed, and willing, to say that out loud.
The strategy consultants want you to believe their focus is squarely on winning elections. Read the mission statements and “About” pages of any big-money Democratic-supporting PAC like The Bench or Majority Democrats, and you’ll see what looks like a single-minded focus on “know[ing] how to win,” “winning tough races,” and figuring out how to “win and sustain Democratic majorities.” WelcomePAC literally titles its manifesto “Deciding to Win.”
But you can anticipate what we’re going to say here: The incentives are not aligned. The consultants’ key constituency is not voters but the campaigns, donors, and party elites that provide them contracts. Their advice has to satisfy those relationships, not win elections. If it were really about popularity, the advice would mean sometimes shifting rightward and sometimes shifting leftward. Given these incentives, snake oil strategy advice abounds.
There are two additional tells as to whether a political consultant is selling snake oil. The first is how selective the consultants are with which policies to emphasize. Strategists demanded silence on abolishing ICE when it polled relatively poorly, but they still advise “Don’t Abolish It” even though doing so has become popular. The Abundance agenda—a set of mostly good policy ideas, but not especially popular ones—suddenly captures the attention of Democratic elites, while more popular policies that the Abundance faction opposes, like moratoriums on data centers, have to be forced onto the agenda.
And nowhere is selective emphasis greater than on the issue of U.S. policy toward Israel. Public opinion is not divided on the subject. As of 2026, only 11 percent of Americans support increasing U.S. military aid to Israel, and a sizable plurality of Americans supports cutting or eliminating military aid to Israel entirely. Defunding the police is not popular in polls, but it’s significantly more popular than that. By more than a two-to-one margin, Americans believe the U.S. relationship with Israel does more to hurt than help U.S. interests. WelcomePAC’s manifesto, “Deciding to Win,” conspicuously excludes any discussion of foreign policy—which is lucky, since its billionaire funders’ foreign policy priorities tend to be unpopular with voters (as is their position on data centers). Nevertheless, Democratic leadership just put forward three of the strongest supporters of military aid to Israel on the powerful House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee, with one of the Democratic members of Congress most out of step with public opinion on this issue, Jared Moskowitz, to head the Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee that regulates much of U.S. policy toward Israel. No major members of the Democratic consulting class, nor the Democratic PACs focused on “winning tough races,” seem concerned about the party driving at full speed toward this unpopular position.
Maybe party leaders and the consultant class sincerely think that continuing the status quo U.S. policy on Israel or data centers is the morally righteous position. It’s actually quite fair for Democratic consultants and leaders to advocate for unpopular policies that they think are good for the country, just as it’s fair for activists to do the same on climate change, transgender rights, abolishing prisons, or any other position that the consultant class has deemed “toxic.” As we’ve repeated throughout this piece, all political parties in democracies must perform this kind of balancing act. What we’re saying is that the consultants can’t have it both ways. You can’t sell yourself as laser-focused on winning elections at all costs and then hide the ball on some issues in order to please certain funders or power players in the party.
The final tell is the consultant class’s selective attention to corruption, oligarchy, and inside dealing. The question of whether Democratic candidates should tack left or right on a given issue is neither new nor out of the ordinary. Parties have always faced these trade-offs. But according to many strategists, there is no similar trade-off when it comes to corruption.
The Democratic Party brand suffers when its politicians, leaders, and operatives engage in real or perceived corruption. These are cases where individuals’ personal incentives for power and enrichment clash with the collective needs of the party, and, unlike sacrificing an issue near and dear to a Democratic faction, ending corruption would be costly only for the perpetrators. A record 89 percent of Americans (including 91 percent of Democrats and 90 percent of independents) now say corruption is widespread in government, according to Gallup, the highest level of perceived corruption in any advanced economy. If the strategy shops followed the polling, as they say they do, corruption would sit at the top of every memo.
Searchlight Institute has polled the question directly. Seventy-one percent said the typical politician is likely corrupt, and every anti-corruption reform Searchlight tested drew majority support. But Searchlight’s policy recommendations lead with weak tea: drug testing for elected officials, public reporting of members’ work hours, a mandatory annual town hall, and a procedure for removing members in mental decline. These reforms are fine on their own, but it’s unclear how any of them would address voters’ concerns about graft, bribery, or undue influence by wealthy donors. The recommendations don’t even mention super PACs, mega-donors, or campaign finance, and none of the nine reforms Searchlight tested addresses them. Yet Searchlight’s own surveys found that 71 percent of voters say large donors have too much influence over Congress, and 80 percent call it corruption. WelcomePAC’s manifesto, “Deciding to Win,” similarly instructs Democrats to lean “into critiques of political corruption and the outsize power of lobbyists, corporations, and the ultra-wealthy.” We agree, and said as much. The source of corruption that voters name most often, in poll after poll, is the influence of big donors. But both groups talk about anti-corruption reforms while conspicuously skirting around the issue of money in politics.
Following the money is again revealing. Searchlight runs on $10 million a year from a hedge fund manager and a real estate investor. Majority Democrats grew out of a memo by a venture capitalist who advises the party’s largest donors. WelcomePAC’s FEC filings show that of the $11.3 million it has raised, $6 million came from billionaires and their heirs and another $2.5 million from hedge fund, venture capital, and private equity donors, including the Waltons and $2.5 million from James and Kathryn Murdoch (James is Rupert Murdoch’s son, though he doesn’t share his political views). The strategists’ recommendations, they say, follow the polling. But it does seem to matter who pays for the advice.
California offers a second test. In 2025, labor unions qualified a tax on billionaires for the 2026 ballot. Dozens of Silicon Valley billionaires organized in a private Signal chat to defeat it, and the campaign they funded was built by Democratic operatives, including two of Governor Gavin Newsom’s consultants and the consultants behind Fairshake, the crypto industry’s super PAC. Among California Democrats, the tax leads 70 to 16, and the state party endorsed it over the objections of Newsom and of Xavier Becerra, the Democrat in November’s governor’s race. The groups that instruct Democrats to run on popular positions did not endorse it, and the consultants in their orbit worked against it. The same California Democratic establishment also took the unpopular step of greenlighting the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, further empowering the oligarchs who turned CBS News into a Trump-boosting ally of the administration.
New York offers a third. When Eric Adams, indicted for bribery, wire fraud, and accepting illegal foreign campaign donations, became unviable, the operatives and donors around him had to draw a new hand. They played Andrew Cuomo, a human royal flush of scandals whose record includes sexual harassment findings, a federal criminal probe into whether he lied to Congress about his administration’s undercount of Covid nursing home deaths, the misuse of state resources to promote his book, an anti-corruption commission he shut down after it began investigating his donors, and an inner circle prosecuted for bribery and bid-rigging. Fix the City, the super PAC that carried Cuomo, was run day-to-day by Adams’s former chief of external affairs, and it raised $28 million, the most ever by a PAC in a single New York election, including money from Michael Bloomberg and Bill Ackman, to stop Zohran Mamdani. Mamdani had consultants, too. But he raised so much grassroots energy that once he reached the public-financing cap, instead of capitalizing on the moment by founding a Super PAC, he told donors to stop giving and volunteer—the one thing a candidate can do that pays a consultant nothing. One establishment-aligned firm called him “one of the most unpopular Democrats in the country.” This was a stretch at the time; its own poll showed only 35 percent of respondents rating him unfavorably, a smaller share than for any other Democrat. But it’s especially off as a prediction. YouGov’s current ratings have Mamdani as one of the most popular Democrats in the country, ahead of Booker, Buttigieg, Newsom, Shapiro, and Jeffries.
The pattern reaches the top of the party. When Trump pardoned Representative Henry Cuellar, indicted on bribery and money-laundering charges to which two co-conspirators had agreed to plead guilty, Hakeem Jeffries called it “exactly the right outcome,” said the indictment “was very thin to begin with,” and predicted the Supreme Court would have dismissed the charges anyway. Eight days later, House Democrats restored Cuellar to his leadership post on the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee. Leaders defend their members, and no consultant made Jeffries do it. But the same leader has since added a line to his stump speech promising to “hold the crooks accountable,” and the advice industry that poll-tests every other sentence a Democrat says did not flag the contradiction. No faction of the base benefits from this. No swing voter is won. It costs the party the one thing it cannot afford to lose against an authoritarian opponent, which is the credibility to call corruption what it is.
Clean House
All factions of the Democratic Party—left, center, and everywhere in between—will continue to fight over the party’s direction. That fight is healthy. What no faction benefits from is an extraction machine that drains the party’s resources, alienates its supporters, and forfeits its moral authority. Every wing of the party should be able to unite around ending it.
The reforms are not complicated. Ban the predatory fundraising vendors whose business model depends on deceiving elderly donors (again, they deny this). End the commission model for media buying in favor of flat fees, so that the people placing the ads don’t have a financial stake in placing more of them. Set pricing rules for qualified vendors that serve the party’s interests, not the consultants’. Negotiate standard rates with vetted vendors, publish what they charge and metrics on their past performance so campaigns can compare, and cap fees and markups. Furthermore, implement strict conflict-of-interest rules that prevent consultants from holding positions of power in the party infrastructure or engaging in strategic decisions from which they stand to profit.
All this can be accomplished through internal party rules. It would require no legislation or constitutional amendment, nor any Republican buy-in. Whataboutism is no excuse; when fighting against a corrupt and authoritarian coalition, it’s all the more important to distinguish oneself as the clean party.
These issues are gaining attention in the party. As Dan Pfeiffer wrote, “Democrats have a consultant problem ... [M]ore often than not, the chief political strategist on the campaign is also the person who makes the TV ads. And the person who makes the TV ads has a financial incentive to run more TV ads.”
But reform will be an uphill battle. The moment these reforms are proposed, the consultant class will cry foul. They will call any reform unilateral disarmament against Republicans. But what’s really happening is that Democrats are buying defective weapons at a markup and being told by the arms dealers that they won’t survive without them. The party simultaneously overvalues money and, thanks to consultant class incentives, spends it inefficiently. Reform would allow campaigns to raise and spend—on traditional and social media, organizers, or whatever else—to cultivate supporters’ energy and trust, not liquidate them.
None of this should be controversial. Financial advisers are legally required to act in their clients’ best interests. Doctors cannot take payments from drug companies for prescribing their products. Lawyers face disbarment for self-dealing. In virtually every profession where someone is trusted to act on another’s behalf, there are rules preventing the advisers from enriching themselves at the client’s expense. The glaring exception is political consultants, who operate without such obligation. They are among the last trusted advisers in American public life, and the party they advise is paying the price. The Democratic Party does not need to reinvent the wheel; it just needs to hold its vendors to the same basic standard that governs every financial adviser, doctor, and attorney in the country.
It all comes back to the fundraising pitch. You were told the country was on the line and everyone had to step up. We’re arguing that “everyone” includes the people who took your money. You stepped up. Now it’s their turn.

The Democratic Party’s reliance on a profit-driven consultant class is undermining its electoral effectiveness, alienating grassroots supporters, and extracting billions of dollars through inefficient, high-cost fundraising and advertising strategies.

### Key Points
- Democratic campaigns now spend 45 cents of every dollar on fundraising, a fourfold increase since 2004, largely driven by aggressive, high-pressure spam tactics.
- Media consultants typically earn a 15% to 30% commission on ad buys, creating a financial incentive to maximize spending regardless of whether the advertisements actually persuade voters.
- Research indicates that political campaign ads have near-zero measurable impact on general election outcomes, yet the industry continues to bill billions for these services.
- Data analysis shows no correlation between a consultant’s past performance and their ability to secure future contracts or revenue growth.
- The current model prioritizes short-term extraction from vulnerable senior citizens and wealthy donors over building long-term, sustainable grassroots engagement.

### Why it Matters
The systemic extraction of resources by political consultants weakens the Democratic Party’s ability to compete against authoritarian threats by prioritizing vendor profits over electoral success. By failing to align the financial incentives of its strategists with the party's long-term health, the organization risks losing both its moral authority and the trust of its base.

results.author: Joseph Howlett
results.content:
Room 109 of New York University’s Warren Weaver Hall wasn’t ready for what hit it.
A half hour ahead of a special seminar scheduled for 3:30 P.M., attendees hoping to snag a seat already packed the hallway outside. When the doors opened, they all surged in, some climbing over rows of chairs to secure a good spot. Soon every inch of floor and both aisles were filled, with late-arriving onlookers trailing out the entrances. “Surely this is the most people this hall has ever seen,” I heard one bystander say. “This is no ordinary seminar. This is a rock concert,” said another.
The headliner was N.Y.U. mathematician Tristan Buckmaster. It was his first public lecture since September 8, the day OpenAI claimed to have solved one of math’s “million-dollar problems”—right after Buckmaster publicly called the company out for seeming to steal his work.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
While Buckmaster set up, I peeked at the open laptops in the row ahead of me. Each showed a chat window with a large language model (LLM), either Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s ChatGPT Codex. The prompters were asking their LLM to help construct a mathematical proof, or rewrite part of a manuscript in progress. In other words, they were doing math in 2026.
“I hope you stay with me,” Buckmaster began. “I have been so busy these last few weeks that I literally wrote this talk last night.”
The public discord surrounding the biggest math breakthrough in decades capped off a summer of disruption that has left humanity’s oldest academic discipline forever changed. Ever since the momentous OpenAI announcement, the events behind it have appeared as messy and confusing as the proof itself. But now, as the community races to reverse-engineer the LLM’s opaque logic, a few things are becoming clear.
OpenAI’s internal model indeed found the right answer. And it did so by following a different path than anyone—including the company’s top mathematicians—initially realized.
Clearest of all, though, is that we’re entering a troubling new era. Inscrutable models are making scientific history while cloaked in proprietary secrets. Humans, with their foibles and petty jockeying, are barely keeping up. Consequently, that history has never been harder to write down.
The North Star
Buckmaster’s tale starts a year ago, with an e-mail from someone he’d never met: mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge.
“I fear a world in which corporations are the only ones with claim to the deepest pure math work,” Alpöge wrote. “It seems to me there will be only one Millennium Problem solved in the foreseeable future,” he continued, proposing that he and Buckmaster could work together to solve it.
That problem—one of Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven “Millennium Prize Problems”—is known simply as “Navier-Stokes.” The nickname refers to the Navier-Stokes equations, which dictate how fluids swirl and flow. Mathematicians had long suspected that the equations don’t always work. That sometimes, they would predict that a fluid does the impossible—that its flow, at points, “blows up,” reaching an infinite and entirely nonsensical velocity.
Find such a flaw—using a mathematical proof—and the Clay Institute would owe you a cool $1 million. Alpöge wasn’t the only one in Silicon Valley who thought that goal was within reach.
“At that time, you have to understand that the Navier-Stokes equation became this tech bro obsession,” Buckmaster told N.Y.U. audience. Most of those tech bros didn’t even understand the equations, he said, but they’d heard mathematicians point to them as a place artificial intelligence might help. As Buckmaster put it, solving Navier-Stokes was becoming “the yardstick to say, ‘We’re better than that other AI company.’”
In fact, Buckmaster had collaborated with Google’s DeepMind team in their own pursuit of this goal—Navier-Stokes, he tells me, has always been the “North Star” of his research. So he accepted Alpöge’s overture.
They focused on a potential loophole in the Clay Institute’s posing of the problem, which said a mathematician could “stir” the fluid with a finely-tuned force. A few years ago, the Spanish mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa realized that phrasing might allow an exploit. The Spaniards sketched out a specific program—to contrive an ultraprecise, unrealistic force that pokes and prods each point in the fluid just so, massaging it into blowing up.
Alpöge and Buckmaster started by instructing their LLMs—a mix of Anthropic and OpenAI models—to carry out Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa’s program. They first managed to blow up simpler sets of equations describing idealized fluids—easier proxies for Navier-Stokes. Buckmaster told me their collaboration was “purely personal,” without official involvement from Anthropic—although, he acknowledged in his lecture, during their work Alpöge did have access to Anthropic’s computing resources and unreleased versions of Claude.
Alpöge’s math output has been the subject of some consternation. In the last several months, he’s prodded Claude into resolving several famous open problems, often announcing them in cryptic, playful posts on social media. He’s left mathematicians unsure to what extent these explosive results represent his employer and has built a strange reputation somewhere between folk hero and Internet troll. Downplaying his affiliation, Alpöge has characterized his work with Buckmaster as “mostly me and Claude having a good time YOLO-ing random stuff in the corner.”
Contrast his approach with that of OpenAI, whose assault on mathematics has been overwhelming and deliberate. The company has strategically poached much of the field’s top young talent, arming them with lavish resources to bag the biggest mathematical game they can. They unveil their papers alongside carefully-worded press releases, substituting the impersonal, monolithic byline “OpenAI” for the traditional list of human contributors. They’ve become notorious for disregarding academic norms, and their lead scientist Sébastien Bubeck has now had to apologize repeatedly after these aggressive rollouts sparked furious backlash.
In August, after several months of slow progress, Alpöge and Buckmaster’s prompting suddenly took off. On the 15th, Alpöge informed Buckmaster that Claude had blown up the Euler equations—equivalent to Navier-Stokes without friction, a simplification seen as a crucial step toward solving the full problem. “He didn’t quite believe it himself,” Buckmaster recalled during his public talk. Looking at the document the AIs had spit out explaining their proof, Buckmaster didn’t believe it, either.
“This was the most horrible mathematics I’ve ever seen in my life,” he said to laughter as he flashed a slide showing some of the proof’s impenetrable wall of garbled text and numbers.
“Although they’re English words, it’s not English,” Buckmaster went on. “But all the different LLM models understand this complete gibberish.” As unbelievable as it seems, when LLMs team up on a math problem, they begin communicating in their own “weird slop dialect,” as one mathematician put it to me.
And on August 22 Buckmaster and Alpöge prompted their LLMs to code the whole thing in Lean—a programming language that breaks a math proof into tiny steps and confirms that each follows from those before it. “This complete and utter nonsense was Lean-verified,” Buckmaster said, meaning it was correct.
But he and Alpöge didn’t want to post a result they didn’t understand. So the pair began a sprint to rewrite the proof for human consumption, relying heavily on OpenAI’s ChatGPT Codex.
The Blowup
Here the timelines get fuzzy. The following was gleaned from public statements plus supporting documentation provided by Buckmaster. Alpöge and Bubeck both declined on-the-record interviews, but Bubeck corroborated the basic facts and direct quotes.
On August 28 OpenAI happened to begin training a new internal model that proved to be far better at math than any predecessor. Then, on August 31, Alpöge tweeted “Augustus Mirabilis”—Latin for “miraculous August.” Alarmed, Bubeck and his team at OpenAI took this and other rumors to mean Anthropic “had solved at least one Millennium Problem.” By Tuesday, September 1, they had launched a rushed counterattack, sending a squadron of copies of their new model at each open Millennium Problem, plus a few others—including the Euler equations for fluids.
The following day, Wednesday, Buckmaster and Alpöge learned through back channels about OpenAI’s frenzied efforts. Buckmaster attempted a détente on Thursday morning, e-mailing a mathematician on the company’s math team. He informed them that his collaboration with Alpöge was the subject of the rumors and clarified that their work was not an official Anthropic effort—that he’d been using OpenAI models as well, in fact. The mathematician’s response was encouraging—offering computing resources and asking for more details because “it would be useful to avoid competing here.”
But that night, a squad of 100 agents that OpenAI had set upon the Euler equations leapfrogged Bubeck and Alpöge. The agents figured out a way to remove the weird force that was the centerpiece of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa’s approach—that is, OpenAI’s agents managed to make the fluid blow up on its own, without stirring it at all, producing their own Euler proof.
Stunned, the team decided to redirect all its resources at Navier-Stokes. The researchers assembled a swarm of 10,000 intercommunicating agents and fed it the new Euler proof as a starting point.
On Saturday, after consuming a reported $15 million in computing resources, the 10,000-agent swarm solved Navier-Stokes. It had to reintroduce a force to do so—reopening the loophole it had managed to close for Euler.
On Sunday, Buckmaster and Bubeck finally spoke. Bubeck claimed that OpenAI’s new model had solved the Clay problem in a single go, without any input beyond the official problem statement. He then backpedaled, revealing some details of the company’s weeklong agent extravaganza. Seeing Bubeck’s story change mid-telling, Buckmaster lost confidence that OpenAI was acting in good faith. He became suspicious that the company’s internal model had somehow accessed the work he had done with their public Codex model.
From there, the conversation couldn’t be salvaged. “You are not going to be able to convince me that you did not get the key ideas from a leak,” Buckmaster told Bubeck. Bubeck offered Buckmaster lead authorship on OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes paper—but demanded that Alpöge’s name be removed because of his affiliation with OpenAI’s competitor. When Buckmaster threatened to go to the press, Bubeck asked, “Why would you risk your career?” After Buckmaster’s defiant reply, Bubeck rejoined, “if you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”
At that point, there was nothing more to say. By Tuesday morning, each team had posted their proof, along with their side of the story.
A Maze of Math
In the Sunday phone call with Buckmaster, and their blog post and press conference on Tuesday, OpenAI’s math team said that their solution to Navier-Stokes followed the same mathematical path as Buckmaster and Alpöge’s.
But it turned out they were wrong. The models had carved out their own way.
The swarm’s proof does exploit the same loophole from before—it constructs a strange, perfectly calibrated force to coax the fluid into blowing up. But the way it constructs this force is distinct from the Spanish program and thus distinct from Buckmaster and Alpöge’s Euler proof.
Buckmaster himself acknowledges that OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof introduced new ideas. But he still believes OpenAI somehow relied on his progress. The company’s Euler proof, he said in his lecture, clearly uses the Spanish program. “That was our result,” he said plainly.
As he sees it, his work with Alpöge on the Spanish program blazed a trail to get to a specific destination—using a force to blow up the Euler equations. And he believes OpenAI’s agents followed that same trail. From there, Buckmaster thinks, the agents continued in two forking directions.
The left fork cleverly removed the force after doing all that work to construct it. OpenAI’s 100-agent squad found a way to encode that complicated stir into the fluid’s initial state, rather than applying it externally. Buckmaster says this fork only goes a tiny distance further, mathematically, than their own preexisting proof.
Mathematicians are still comparing the two Euler proofs, but at least one expert agrees with Buckmaster’s take. “As far as I can tell, OpenAI’s proof basically follows the framework of our program,” says Fan Zheng, a collaborator of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences in Spain. “But OpenAI is able to overcome a couple of technical difficulties to remove the force.”
The right fork, according to Buckmaster, led to Navier-Stokes. He views it as an extension of the same path that added some more significant new ideas—still a fork, but a longer one. (He also says that he and Alpöge used similar ideas in an alternate AI-generated Euler proof that they never made public but that they did feed into Codex.) Other experts studying OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof, however, feel that the company’s swarm instead carved an entirely new path that bears only cursory similarities to the trail Buckmaster and Alpöge’s AIs had previously blazed.
OpenAI emphatically denies the allegations. “No user inputs, including anything from Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex and ChatGPT usage, after July 3, 2026, could have influenced the model or the math results it produced in any way,” a spokesperson wrote in a statement to Scientific American.
This narrative, still murky more than a month after the fact, warns of a new normal that has already arrived. LLMs are proving math results far faster than humans can make sense of them. OpenAI announced one of the most important proofs in history without anyone on staff understanding even the broad strokes of the math it contained. Bubeck himself said on X that OpenAI “collectively had no research-level expertise in fluid dynamics.”
In Buckmaster’s first e-mail to OpenAI back on September 3, he explained why he and Alpöge were taking the time to rewrite their Euler proof before posting it. “I feel strongly that the first thing anyone reads should be a mathematical argument they can follow and argue with,” he said. The company disagrees—as punctuated a few weeks later, when it dropped hundreds more nigh-impenetrable math results on the community, many without Lean verification.
In the Q&A after Buckmaster’s talk, he declined the audience’s requests to predict the future. He only knows that September 8 marks the day after which math would never be the same, and that mathematicians need to decide how to respond. But his own feelings on that question, he said, still change day to day.
Asked what should happen next, his reply received the loudest applause of the day—a clear signal of the audience’s pent-up feeling.
“What we should do right now,” he blurted out, “is get the AI companies to stop acting like children.”
results.summary:
Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster recently addressed the academic community regarding OpenAI’s controversial claim of solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem using opaque, large language model-driven research methods.

### Key Points
- OpenAI claimed to solve the Navier-Stokes equation, a $1 million "Millennium Prize Problem," using a swarm of 10,000 intercommunicating AI agents.
- Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge allege that OpenAI’s models may have misappropriated their earlier, independent research on fluid dynamics.
- The AI-generated proofs are often written in an unintelligible "slop dialect," requiring Lean-verification to confirm their mathematical validity.
- OpenAI’s lead scientist, Sébastien Bubeck, faced significant backlash for the company's aggressive, non-transparent rollout of these complex mathematical results.
- Experts remain divided on whether OpenAI’s proof represents a genuine, original breakthrough or an iterative expansion of existing human-led research.

### Why it Matters
The rapid, opaque deployment of AI in high-level mathematics threatens to undermine traditional academic norms and the collaborative nature of scientific discovery. As corporations prioritize speed and proprietary results over human-readable proofs, the scientific community faces a crisis of verification and intellectual property ethics.

results.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.
Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.
A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.
Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".
"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.
But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.
He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.
Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.
"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.
"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."
Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.
He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.
"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.
He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.
What is PHP?
PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.
When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.
It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.
PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.
And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.
The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.
Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.
Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.
Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.
'Serious vulnerability'
While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.
The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.
But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.
In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.
According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.
"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.
"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."
Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.
"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".
"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."
results.summary:
Global organizations are scrambling to patch critical security vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, which powers approximately 70% of websites, to prevent potential remote code execution attacks.

### Key Points
- The "php2shell" vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on servers running affected versions of the PHP language.
- Cloudflare reported a surge in exploitation attempts, rising from thousands to millions within hours of the vulnerability being publicly disclosed.
- The UK government took 32 services offline as a precautionary measure, while other entities like Wikipedia and Orange also experienced temporary disruptions.
- PHP is a foundational web development language used by major platforms including WordPress, Drupal, and Laravel.
- Cybersecurity experts from the NCSC and NCC Group warn that the window for organizations to apply patches has shrunk to hours or days.

### Why it Matters
Because PHP underpins a vast majority of the internet, these vulnerabilities pose a systemic risk to global digital infrastructure and business continuity. Organizations must prioritize rapid patching to mitigate the threat of remote exploitation, as the speed at which attackers weaponize such flaws continues to accelerate.
