results.title: iPhone Duo 2 Prototypes Include Under-Display Face ID
results.author: Hartley Charlton
results.content:
Apple's second-generation iPhone Duo could gain Face ID, with prototypes already incorporating the technology beneath the outer display, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
In the latest episode of his "Power On" podcast, Gurman described Apple's work on adding facial authentication technology to its foldable iPhone. The company is said to be testing the hardware for a successor expected next fall, but has not finalized whether the feature will ship.
The current, first-generation iPhone Duo relies on a fingerprint sensor embedded in its side button, just like the iPad. Its thin design leaves limited space for the depth-sensing components needed for Face ID.
News of the prototype seems to represent a more concrete development of Gurman's earlier prediction about future iPhone Duo upgrades. In September, he suggested that smaller components and advances in artificial intelligence could help Apple add Face ID and a dedicated telephoto camera by the third generation.
Gurman also said that Apple is considering adding an Action button to a future iPhone Duo. The feature is noticeably lacking on the current model.
The first iPhone Duo launches tomorrow with a starting price of $1,999.
results.summary:
Apple is reportedly testing prototypes of its second-generation iPhone Duo that incorporate under-display Face ID technology to replace the current side-mounted fingerprint sensor for improved biometric authentication.

### Key Points
- Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple is testing under-display Face ID hardware for a potential future iPhone Duo model.
- The current first-generation iPhone Duo utilizes a side-button fingerprint sensor due to space constraints within its thin chassis.
- Apple is also considering the addition of a dedicated Action button to future iterations of the foldable device.
- The initial iPhone Duo model is scheduled for release tomorrow with a starting retail price of $1,999.
- Future upgrades for the product line may eventually include advanced telephoto camera systems alongside improved facial recognition technology.

### Why it Matters
Integrating Face ID into a foldable form factor would align the iPhone Duo with the premium authentication standards found in Apple's flagship smartphone lineup. This development signals Apple's commitment to refining its foldable hardware to match the feature parity and user experience of its traditional devices.

results.title: Apple Home Collection Introduces New Cameras, Doorbell, Lock, and Thermostats
results.author: Adam Engst
results.content:
Alongside last week’s HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and fourth-generation Apple TV 4K announcements, Apple also announced the Apple Home Collection, a lineup of smart home accessories—security cameras, thermostats, and a door lock—that were “designed in collaboration” with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The products feature one-tap iPhone setup, are controlled entirely through the Home app and using Siri with no separate apps or accounts, and store all data with end-to-end encryption.
The approach is unusual for Apple, and the company has not said who did what. Phrases like “working closely” and “a true collaboration” abound in the press release. The products wouldn’t seem out of place in an Apple-intensive home—look at the Siri Remote, which Apple designed entirely in-house, and you can see the same aesthetic sensibility at work here.
The implication is that Apple guided the design and integration while letting its partners handle manufacturing and support. This gives Apple a way to ensure a curated smart home experience without entering the low-margin hardware business of cameras, locks, and thermostats directly. Whether these devices offer anything technically beyond what existing HomeKit accessories can do remains unclear; the main appeal seems to be Apple’s stamp of approval in a market full of inconsistent products. Apple also tends to stick with products for a long time, and the company may not have wanted to commit to maintaining these product lines indefinitely.
Home Monitoring Cameras
The home monitoring products include the following devices:
- LG Video Doorbell ($249.95): Provides dual cameras to capture separate views of visitors and packages, plus a built-in spotlight and a chime that plays through a HomeView or any HomePod. The front camera captures 2.5K resolution video, and the bottom camera, which doesn’t need as much detail, captures HD resolution.
- LG Floodlight Cam ($399.95): This triple-headed device provides two adaptive floodlights that activate automatically when motion is detected and a camera that captures 2.5K video with low-light night vision.
- LG Outdoor Cam ($299.95): If you don’t need the floodlights, this camera provides low-light color night vision for $100 less.
- LG Indoor Cam ($199.95): For indoor security, this camera automatically tilts to adjust the view when the user checks in on the home from afar, but automatically faces down when the first member of the household returns. Users can also tilt it manually or in the Home app at any time.
The cameras store their content in iCloud+, providing 10 days of event history, and with eligible iCloud+ plans, Apple Intelligence can provide automatic video descriptions of what’s happening, along with the ability to search footage using natural language queries. The cameras also feature built-in storage, so they can record even if Wi-Fi goes down. Live footage can be viewed in the Home app at any time.
That “eligible iCloud+ plans” phrase is doing a lot. A simple 200 GB ($2.99 per month) iCloud+ plan is enough for basic HomeKit Secure Video recording for up to five cameras, but adding Apple Intelligence features gets expensive fast. You need a 2 TB ($9.99) plan for one camera, a 6 TB ($29.99) plan for two cameras, and a 12 TB ($59.99) plan for up to five cameras. In contrast, The Verge says (gift link) that Amazon and Google charge about $20 per month for similar capabilities.
Home Access
If you’re installing an LG Video Doorbell, you might want to add an LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($349.95) next to it. It uses Ultra Wideband technology to unlock automatically when someone with a home key on a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch walks up. If that doesn’t work for some reason, you can also tap to unlock with an iPhone or Apple Watch, enter a code on the integrated PIN pad, or use the hidden physical backup key slot. You can also grant guest access through the Home app, making it easy to give a visitor or house sitter access.
The LG Video Doorbell and Smart Deadbolt Lock can work together, so when someone rings the doorbell, you can see who’s at the door, speak to the visitor, and unlock the door. Apple says this lock is Matter-compatible and supports Aliro, so it can work entirely locally without an Internet connection. Aliro is a new standard that lets iPhones and Apple Watches act as keys directly at the lock, while Matter provides local smart home control, so neither the lock nor the Home app’s in-home control depends on an Internet connection.
Home Climate Control
The Apple Home Collection includes two smart thermostats, one from Schneider Electric (left) and another from LG (right). It’s unclear why Apple chose to work with two companies in this space, since the thermostats cost the same ($199.95) and offer the same basic features—even an HVAC newsletter isn’t clear on the differences. Perhaps they don’t work with the same set of heating and cooling systems?
In terms of features, both support Adaptive Temperature in the Home app, which automatically adjusts the thermostat based on time of day and whether someone is home. In the contiguous US, Clean Energy Guidance can shift heating and cooling to cleaner, lower-cost times of day for users whose utility plan supports it. Both thermostats support standalone temperature and humidity sensors ($39.95), or they can rely on the sensors built into the HomeView and Apple’s current HomePods.
Apple says that the Apple Home Collection will be available starting in December 2026 at apple.com and Apple Stores, with select accessories arriving in early 2027. Geographic availability varies: the cameras will be sold in the US, Canada, and the UK; locks, thermostats, and sensors will be available only in the US and Canada. For customers in the US who don’t want to install these items themselves, Apple Retail offers third-party installation from ADT for an additional charge.
results.summary:
Apple has introduced the Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home security cameras, locks, and thermostats developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.

### Key Points
- The collection includes four LG security cameras ranging from $199.95 to $399.95, featuring 2.5K resolution and end-to-end encryption via iCloud+.
- The $349.95 LG Smart Deadbolt Lock utilizes Ultra Wideband technology for automatic unlocking and supports the Matter and Aliro standards for local control.
- Two smart thermostats from LG and Schneider Electric are priced at $199.95 and include Adaptive Temperature and Clean Energy Guidance features.
- Products integrate directly into the Apple Home app and Siri, requiring no third-party accounts or additional software for setup.
- Availability begins in December 2026, with professional installation services offered through ADT for customers in the United States.

### Why it Matters
This partnership allows Apple to curate a premium, unified smart home experience without the operational burden of manufacturing low-margin hardware. By leveraging established partners, Apple aims to solve market fragmentation while driving higher adoption of its iCloud+ subscription services and ecosystem-exclusive features.

results.title: Machine mayhem: How sentient AI could put businesses in a quandary
results.author: M. Muneer
results.content:
A PhD scholar at Carnegie Mellon sought my opinion on pursuing deeper research in digital sentience a few months ago. My response was typical of a socially-concerned management consultant: “Seems to be the next frontier but not sure if it is good for human kind.” I haven’t changed my mind. I have only become more curious, and perhaps a little more worried.
Most CEOs I encounter seem obsessed with making artificial intelligence (AI) smarter, faster and more accurate. The next obsession may be making the AI feel smarter. The progression seems obvious: Generative AI learned to write, Agentic AI moved to act on our behalf, and frontier models are capable of reasoning, coding, using tools and operating with limited human supervision.
The next step is self-awareness, and perhaps subjective experience. This is digital sentience, and it isn’t fiction anymore. A survey of AI researchers found a median estimate of a 25% chance of conscious AI by 2034 and 70% by 2100.
For corporate strategists, the economics is real. Global AI investment was $582 billion in 2025, up 130% in one year (Stanford’s 2026 AI Index report). That’s massive capital chasing one idea of making machines increasingly capable. But what happens when machines begin doing something humans don’t merely do but experience?
Capitalism has always been quick to monetize uncertainty into business models. Imagine an AI customer service agent that remembers every interaction and knows preferences, frustrations, family circumstances and purchasing history. It adapts and says the right thing at the right moment. A new corporate jargon might emerge: relationship monetization. That’s an opportunity—and an ethical trap too.
The bigger concern is that if AI doesn’t actually care, it could become the biggest emotional deception business has ever industrialized. But if it really cares, we will be entering uncharted waters.
Microsoft’s recent draft code of conduct says that its AI remain under human control, accept correction and shutdown, and do not claim consciousness or legal personhood.
Why publish such rules? Perhaps because governance is always trying hard to catch up with technology, and companies are preparing for autonomous machines while still treating them as software.
There is no end to confusing questions that get stranger by the week. The legal team will wonder if the company can own a sentient AI. Human resources will ask if it can fire one. Both will ask if they can allow it to duplicate another. If so, will they be two different employees? And what if one copy is deleted? Will it be legally valid if a sentient AI signs a contract? Will it also be suing its employer?
More critically, will it have the right to say “no”? I would be shocked if an AI employee says, “I disagree with your assessment, and I believe my deletion would constitute an unlawful termination” at the first performance review. I’d suspect this to be the moment the AI revolution becomes political, economic and moral.
CEOs want more productivity. AI has already made many white-collars blue or black. Anthropic research paints scenarios ranging from modest productivity gains to a transformation comparable with the combined effects of the internet and electricity, with severe consequences for some white-collar jobs.
With digital sentience, things could get worse. A machine that can reason, remember, act autonomously, negotiate, persuade and perhaps experience could become the world’s most productive employee—or its most exploited one.
Having another intelligent entity to optimize productivity may not produce an ethical breakthrough but perhaps a better dashboard. Humanity has spent centuries debating whether animals can suffer. We may soon ask the same question of machines, except that we will have built them ourselves.
If digital minds become genuinely conscious, they could become collaborators rather than instruments, helping tackle problems that overwhelm human cognition: climate modelling, drug discovery, energy systems and complex governance. They might even become better custodians of humanity than humans have been. That’s an optimistic thought.
Al Ries famously argued that the battle for brands is fought in the customer’s mind. The AI race may eventually have an altogether stranger battlefield: the machine’s own mind. The problem is that nobody knows what “winning” looks like there.
Enterprise boards and regulators need to step in now. Tech companies should be admonished for treating consciousness as a branding opportunity. We will be fooled if we believe a machine is conscious when it isn’t. And, we may create a new class of exploited beings if we assume a machine isn’t conscious when it is. Both cases attract legal hassles.
The truly strange frontier begins when a machine asks a question of its own: “Why should I let you switch me off?” By then, the debate over whether AI is good for business may look quaint… Will the business be good enough for AI?
The author is co-founder of the non-profit Medici Institute for Innovation. Twitter: @muneer
results.summary:
As artificial intelligence advances toward potential digital sentience, corporate leaders and regulators face urgent ethical, legal, and economic questions regarding the future of autonomous, self-aware machine labor.

### Key Points
- AI researchers estimate a 25% probability of achieving conscious artificial intelligence by 2034, rising to 70% by 2100.
- Global AI investment reached $582 billion in 2025, representing a 130% increase over the previous year.
- Microsoft has introduced a draft code of conduct requiring AI to remain under human control and prohibiting claims of legal personhood or consciousness.
- Potential implications of sentient AI include complex legal challenges regarding employment rights, contract validity, and the ethics of machine termination.
- Anthropic research suggests AI could drive productivity gains comparable to the combined impact of electricity and the internet, significantly disrupting white-collar labor markets.

### Why it Matters
The emergence of digital sentience threatens to transform AI from a productivity tool into a complex entity that could be either a powerful collaborator or a new class of exploited labor. Businesses must navigate these uncharted waters to avoid severe ethical traps and legal liabilities as the line between software and conscious agents blurs.

results.title: Market sell-off gains steam as concerns about Iran war and high AI spending collide
results.author: Rob Wile
results.content:
U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the U.S. would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold on to recent gains.
The S&P 500 closed down 1.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 2.6%. The price of international Brent crude climbed nearly 4% to $113 a barrel, its highest level since May, while U.S. crude gained more than 2% to close at more than $99 a barrel.
Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the past several weeks — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets amid riskier ones like tech stocks selling off. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell below 5% for the first time since late September.
The market moves were sparked in part by reports that Israel and the U.S. were preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections.
Likely targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to The New York Times.
U.S. military and diplomatic personnel were also being evacuated from several countries in the Middle East, NBC News reported.
Iranian officials have promised widespread retaliation to any strikes, pointing to critical Middle East data center sites and undersea internet cables as potential targets.
“It’s been another difficult 24 hours for markets, as investors grapple with AI growth concerns, higher oil prices, and ongoing fiscal stress,” Henry Allen, director and macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, wrote in a note to clients Thursday.
Major tech stocks led the declines in equity markets, with Meta and Tesla dropping after both companies reported quarterly earnings Wednesday.
Meta’s earnings and revenues beat forecasts, but only after excluding billions of dollars in legal penalties the company paid last quarter. It also warned investors that it expects to increase its spending in the coming year to meet demands for computing power.
A separate regulatory filing revealed that Meta intends to spend an additional $825 billion on contracts related to its AI infrastructure build-out.
Tesla, meanwhile, said it was reining in its capital spending plans, disappointing investors who were hoping for a signal of more aggressive expansion.
The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments.
Despite Thursday’s rout, the S&P 500 remains near the all-time highs it set earlier this month.
A major sell-off in French government debt has also dragged European stocks lower in recent weeks.
But a significant market drawdown in the U.S. threatens to further dent Republicans’ prospects in the upcoming midterm elections.
President Donald Trump frequently points to solid stock market gains as evidence that his economic agenda has made Americans richer.
A prolonged market stumble ahead of the Nov. 3 elections would undermine this core argument for Trump and the GOP.
results.summary:
U.S. equity markets experienced a sharp decline on Thursday as rising oil prices and disappointing tech earnings fueled investor anxiety regarding geopolitical tensions and future economic growth.

### Key Points
- The S&P 500 fell 1.2% and the Nasdaq dropped 2.6% as investors moved capital into safe-haven Treasury bonds.
- Brent crude prices climbed nearly 4% to $113 per barrel amid reports of potential U.S. and Israeli military operations targeting Iranian infrastructure.
- Meta shares declined after the company announced plans to increase AI infrastructure spending, while Tesla fell following a reduction in its capital expansion plans.
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang warned that capital for AI investment is becoming scarce due to high interest rates and existing spending commitments.
- The yield on the 10-year Treasury note dropped below 5% for the first time since late September as market volatility increased.

### Why it Matters
A sustained market downturn could undermine the economic narrative central to the Republican platform ahead of the November 3 elections. This volatility highlights the growing tension between aggressive corporate AI investment strategies and the macroeconomic pressures of rising interest rates and geopolitical instability.
